---
title: "Dropback Concepts: Smash, Flood, Mesh, Levels, Dagger, and Four Verticals"
subtitle: "The two- and three-receiver combinations behind almost every pass thrown more than ten yards, and how a quarterback reads each one"
description: "What a pass concept is and why offenses think in concepts rather than routes; the four ways a concept puts the defense in a bind (vertical stretch, horizontal stretch, triangle, man-beater); fourteen dropback concepts drawn as plates with numbered progressions (smash, flood, levels, curl-flat, drive, shallow cross, dagger, Y-cross, mesh, angle, four verticals, post-wheel, scissors, yankee); rub routes and where they become illegal picks; tags and route conversions; and where on the field the passing game earns its value."
glossary:
  "Pass concept": "A set of routes designed to work together on one pass play, usually by putting one or two defenders in a position where whatever they do leaves a receiver open. Concepts have names (smash, flood, mesh) so the whole offense can learn one word instead of five routes."
  Smash: "A two-receiver concept on one side: the outside receiver runs a short hitch and the inside receiver a corner route over the top of him. A high-low read of the cornerback, built to beat Cover 2, in which the cornerback sits short."
  Flood: {def: "A three-receiver concept that puts three receivers at three depths near one sideline (a deep route, an intermediate out or sail route, and a flat route), so two defenders face three receivers.", aliases: ["Sail"]}
  Levels: "A concept in which two receivers on the same side run in-breaking routes at two depths (a short in at about 5 yards and a dig at about 12), a high-low read of the linebacker between them."
  Mesh: "A concept in which two receivers from opposite sides run shallow crossing routes that pass within a yard or two of each other over the middle, so defenders chasing them in man coverage run into traffic. Against zone, the crossers settle in the holes."
  "Rub route": {def: "A route designed to cross close to a teammate's route, so a defender chasing one of the receivers has to go around the other. Legal while the receiver simply runs his route; when he deliberately blocks a defender more than a yard past the line of scrimmage before the ball is touched, it is an illegal pick (offensive pass interference).", aliases: ["Pick route"]}
  "Drive (concept)": "A concept in which one receiver runs a shallow cross at 2–4 yards and a teammate from the same side runs a dig at about 12 yards behind him, a high-low read of the linebacker in the middle."
  "Shallow cross": "A concept built around a receiver running a crossing route at about 5 yards under a dig or 'sit' route coming from the other side at 10–12 yards: a high-low read of the middle linebacker, and a route that runs away from man defenders. A staple of the Air Raid."
  "Curl-flat": "A concept pairing a curl at 10–12 yards with a flat route underneath, often with a third receiver settling in a hook route inside: a high-low read of the defender covering the curl and the flat."
  Dagger: "A concept in which the inside receiver runs straight up the seam to pull the underneath and deep defenders away, and the outside receiver runs a deep dig (15–18 yards) into the space they leave. Built to beat two-high coverages."
  "Y-cross": "An Air Raid concept in which a receiver from one side (traditionally the Y) runs a deep crossing route to the far side at 15–18 yards, under a go route that clears the cornerback and over a flat route: a three-level stretch built from across the field."
  "Four verticals": "A concept in which four receivers run straight up the field at once, two outside and two up the seams, so the defense's two or three deep defenders face four deep routes."
  "Post-wheel": "A two-receiver concept on one side: the outside receiver runs a post toward the middle and the inside receiver (or a back) runs a wheel up the sideline, stretching the deep defender on that side inside and outside."
  Yankee: "A two-receiver deep shot, usually off play-action with max protection: a post from one side and a deep over route (a crosser at about 18–22 yards) from the other, a high-low read of the single deep safety."
  "Angle route": {def: "A running back's route that starts toward the flat, as if on a swing or flat route, then snaps back inside and upfield under the linebackers. Built to beat a linebacker covering the back in man coverage.", aliases: ["Texas route"]}
  Scissors: "A two-receiver deep concept on one side in which the outside receiver runs a post and the inside receiver a corner route, so their paths cross (like the blades of scissors). Built to stretch the safety and cornerback in two-high coverages such as Quarters."
  "Man-beater": "A pass concept designed to beat man coverage, usually by crossing routes, rubs, or routes that break away from a defender's leverage, rather than by stretching a zone defender."
  "Route conversion": "A rule built into a route that changes it according to the coverage: for example, a seam route that stays straight against one deep safety but bends into the open middle against two."
  "Triangle read": "A three-receiver read in which the receivers form a triangle around two underneath defenders, one route high and two low (or two high and one low), so the quarterback has a high-low and an inside-outside choice at once."
---

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (shared drawing helpers for this chapter)"
#| output: false
import os
import logging
import shutil

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, Polygon, RegularPolygon, Patch, Rectangle
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

import gridiron.play as gplay
from contextlib import contextmanager
from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, routes as r, style

logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
style.apply()
PDF = os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")
READ_GREEN = "#0f7a55"   # a darker step of the aqua highlight, for text, numbers and read lines
GREY = style.MUTED
OD, DD = style.OFFENSE_DARK, style.DEFENSE_DARK
LINE_D, OFF_BALL, GUN, UNDER = -0.7, -1.5, -5.0, -1.9
LOS = 40  # the offense's own 30: room to draw deep routes


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- players and alignments
def O(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=key if label is None else label)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def line5():
    """The five offensive linemen, 1.6 yards apart (only the center is lettered)."""
    return [O(k, k, LINE_D, w, "C" if k == "C" else "") for k, w in
            (("LT", -3.2), ("LG", -1.6), ("C", 0.0), ("RG", 1.6), ("RT", 3.2))]


def spread(rb_w=-1.5, x_w=-15.0, h_w=-9.0, y_w=9.0, z_w=15.0):
    """11 personnel, shotgun 2x2. X and Z on the line (with the five linemen: seven on the line);
    H in the left slot and Y, a tight end split out, in the right slot, both a step off the ball."""
    return line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", GUN, rb_w, "R"),
                      O("X", "WR", LINE_D, x_w), O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, h_w),
                      O("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, y_w), O("Z", "WR", LINE_D, z_w)]


def dline(s=1):
    return [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -5.4 * s, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.8 * s, "T"),
            D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.4 * s, "T"), D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.4 * s, "E")]


def _apply(players, extra):
    extra = extra or {}
    return [q.moved(d=extra[q.key][0], w=extra[q.key][1]) if q.key in extra else q for q in players]


def cover3(nb_side=1, extra=None):
    """4-2-5 nickel, Cover 3 against 2x2: corners off with outside leverage, one deep safety, and a
    curl-flat defender over each slot: the nickel ($) on side nb_side (+1 = offense's right), the
    strong safety on the other."""
    s = nb_side
    return _apply(dline() + [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.8, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.2, "W"),
                             D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -16.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 16.0, "CB"),
                             D("NB", "NB", 5.0, s * 7.2, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 5.5, -s * 7.2, "SS"),
                             D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.0, "FS")], extra)


def cover2(extra=None):
    """4-2-5 nickel, Cover 2: corners squatting at 5 yards with outside leverage, two deep safeties."""
    return _apply(dline() + [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.6, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -4.2, "W"),
                             D("NB", "NB", 4.5, 6.6, "$"),
                             D("LCB", "CB", 5.0, -16.3, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 5.0, 16.3, "CB"),
                             D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -8.5, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 12.5, 8.5, "SS")], extra)


def quarters(extra=None):
    """4-2-5 nickel, Quarters (Cover 4): corners off, two safeties at about 10 yards reading the slots."""
    return _apply(dline() + [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.6, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -4.2, "W"),
                             D("NB", "NB", 4.5, 6.6, "$"),
                             D("LCB", "CB", 7.5, -16.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.5, 16.0, "CB"),
                             D("FS", "FS", 10.0, -7.5, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 10.0, 7.5, "SS")], extra)


def cover1(extra=None):
    """Nickel Cover 1 (man-free): corners pressed, the nickel on H, the strong safety on Y, the Will
    on the back, the Mike free to rush or sit in the hole, one deep safety."""
    return _apply(dline() + [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 0.8, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.6, "W"),
                             D("NB", "NB", 1.6, -8.3, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 4.5, 8.0, "SS"),
                             D("LCB", "CB", 1.3, -14.3, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 1.3, 14.3, "CB"),
                             D("FS", "FS", 13.5, 0.0, "FS")], extra)


def protect(p, rushers=("WDE", "WDT", "SDT", "SDE"), depth=1.2, rush=1.6, linemen=("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT")):
    """Linemen set, four rushers engage them: enough to say 'pass', no more."""
    for k in linemen:
        p.block(k, pts=[(-depth, 0.0)])
    for k in rushers:
        if k in p.players:
            p.rush(k, pts=[(-rush, 0.0)], speed=2.0)


def go_to(p, key, end, kind="path", delay=0.0, speed=None, via=()):
    """Move `key` through absolute (d, w) points `via` to `end`."""
    start = np.array(p._cur(key))
    pts = [tuple(np.array(q) - start) for q in (*via, end)]
    if kind == "rush":
        return p.rush(key, pts=pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    if kind == "route":
        return p.route(key, pts, frame="field", delay=delay, speed=speed)
    if kind == "block":
        return p.block(key, pts=pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    return {"path": p.path, "run": p.run}[kind](key, pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)


def route_to(p, key, *pts, delay=0.0, speed=None):
    """A route through absolute (d, w) points."""
    return go_to(p, key, pts[-1], kind="route", via=pts[:-1], delay=delay, speed=speed)


SWING_NUM = {-1: (-4.4, -14.6), 1: (-4.4, 14.6)}


def swing(p, side=-1, key="RB"):
    """The back checks for a blitzer, then swings wide behind the slot: the checkdown.
    Returns where to put his progression number."""
    route_to(p, key, (-4.8, side * 4.5), (-4.2, side * 10.5), (-3.0, side * 13.0), delay=0.4)
    return SWING_NUM[side]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- drawing helpers
def _P(fld, p, d, w):
    return fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))


def clean(ax):
    """Drop the painted yard numbers (they sit where receivers stand); clip all text to the window."""
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_text().isdigit() and t.get_alpha() == 0.55:
            t.remove()
        else:
            t.set_clip_on(True)


def ruler(fld, p, fs=6.0, step=5, top=30):
    """Depth labels (yards past the line of scrimmage) just inside the left edge of the window."""
    xl = (160 / 3) - fld.y1 + 0.4
    for d in range(step, top + 1, step):
        y = p.los + d
        if fld.x0 + 1.5 <= y <= fld.x1 - 1.5:
            fld.ax.text(xl, y, f"{d}" + (" yd" if d == step else ""), fontsize=fs, color=style.INK_2,
                        ha="left", va="center", zorder=12,
                        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.12", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.85))


def draw(p, width_in=8.3, ax=None, show_ruler=True, **kw):
    """Draw a play without a title. A stand-alone field gets ~6.4 in of drawing width after the
    default subplot margins are cropped (width_in is the figure width before cropping)."""
    fld = p.draw(width_in=width_in, ax=ax, title=False, **kw)
    clean(fld.ax)
    if show_ruler:
        ruler(fld, p)
    return fld


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7.0, ha="center", weight="normal", box=True):
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(float(x), float(y), text, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=13,
                fontweight=weight, linespacing=1.15,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9) if box else None)


def point_to(fld, p, text_at, target, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7, ha="center"):
    (xt, yt), (xp, yp) = _P(fld, p, *text_at), _P(fld, p, *target)
    fld.ax.annotate(text, (float(xp), float(yp)), xytext=(float(xt), float(yt)), fontsize=fontsize,
                    color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=13, linespacing=1.15,
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=color, lw=0.7, shrinkA=2, shrinkB=7),
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9))


def branch(fld, p, pts, color=READ_GREEN, lw=1.7, dash=(0, (3, 2.2)), end="arrow", z=5):
    """A dashed path through absolute (d, w) points: a defender's reaction, or the other branch of a read."""
    xs, ys = _P(fld, p, np.array([q[0] for q in pts]), np.array([q[1] for q in pts]))
    fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=color, lw=lw, ls=dash, zorder=z, solid_capstyle="round")
    if end == "arrow":
        fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[-2], ys[-2]), (xs[-1], ys[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                         mutation_scale=10, color=color, lw=lw, zorder=z))


def ghost(fld, p, pts):
    """A route that is part of the call but not part of the read: drawn faint grey."""
    branch(fld, p, pts, color="#a9a8a1", lw=1.4, dash="-", z=3.6)


def taken(fld, p, pts, lw=1.4):
    """A route the defender has taken away: grey, dashed, with an X at the end."""
    branch(fld, p, pts, color=GREY, lw=lw, dash=(0, (2, 2)), end="none")
    x, y = _P(fld, p, *pts[-1])
    fld.ax.plot([float(x)], [float(y)], marker="X", ms=8, color=DD, mec="white", mew=0.7, zorder=9)


def opening(fld, p, center, size, color=style.THIRD):
    """A soft green oval: the throwing window that opens."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, *center)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Ellipse((float(x), float(y)), size[1], size[0], fc=color, alpha=0.2, ec=color, lw=1.0,
                             zorder=1.6))


def triangle(fld, p, pts, color=style.THIRD):
    xy = [tuple(float(v) for v in _P(fld, p, *q)) for q in pts]
    fld.ax.add_patch(Polygon(xy, closed=True, fc=color, alpha=0.15, ec=color, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (4, 2)), zorder=1.7))


def bracket(fld, p, d, w0, w1, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7, dy=1.2):
    """A horizontal dimension line at depth d from w0 to w1, labelled above."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, p, d, w0), _P(fld, p, d, w1)
    fld.ax.annotate("", (float(x1), float(y1)), xytext=(float(x0), float(y0)),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=color, lw=0.8), zorder=6)
    if text:
        say(fld, p, d + dy, (w0 + w1) / 2, text, color=color, fontsize=fontsize)


def num(fld, p, n, at, color=READ_GREEN, fs=7.6):
    """A progression number: the order of the quarterback's looks."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, *at)
    fld.ax.text(float(x), float(y), str(n), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color="white",
                fontweight="bold", zorder=14,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="circle,pad=0.22", fc=color, ec="white", lw=0.8))


def tag(fld, p, text, fontsize=7.4):
    """The stretch label, top right of a plate."""
    fld.ax.text(0.985, 0.975, text, transform=fld.ax.transAxes, ha="right", va="top", fontsize=fontsize,
                color=style.INK, fontweight="bold", zorder=15,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.3", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.6))


def panel_title(ax, text, fs=9):
    ax.set_title(text, fontsize=fs, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")


LEGEND = {
    "route": Line2D([], [], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.8, label="route"),
    "ghost": Line2D([], [], color="#a9a8a1", lw=1.4, label="route outside the read"),
    "block": Line2D([], [], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.8, marker="|", ms=8, mew=2.2, label="block"),
    "run": Line2D([], [], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=2.6, label="ball carrier / fake"),
    "pass": Line2D([], [], color=style.BALL, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (2, 2)), label="the throw"),
    "drop": Line2D([], [], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (3, 2)), label="defender's drop"),
    "man": Line2D([], [], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (1, 2)), label="man assignment"),
    "react": Line2D([], [], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (3, 2.2)), label="defender's reaction"),
    "num": Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", ms=9, mfc=READ_GREEN, mec="white", label="progression (1 = first look)"),
    "ring": Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", ms=11, mfc="none", mec=style.THIRD, mew=2, label="defender in conflict"),
    "window": Patch(fc=style.THIRD, alpha=0.25, ec=style.THIRD, label="window that opens"),
    "taken": Line2D([], [], color=GREY, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (2, 2)), marker="X", ms=7, mfc=DD,
                    mec="white", label="taken away"),
}


def legend(fig, keys, ncol=None, y=0.0, fs=7):
    hs = [LEGEND[k] for k in keys]
    fig.legend(handles=hs, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, y), ncol=ncol or min(len(hs), 4), fontsize=fs,
               frameon=False, handlelength=2.0, columnspacing=1.0)


PLATE_KEYS = ["route", "ghost", "drop", "num", "ring"]


def field_legend(ax, keys, fs=7.2):
    """Legend tucked just under a single field."""
    hs = [LEGEND[k] for k in keys]
    ax.legend(handles=hs, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0), ncol=len(hs) if len(hs) <= 4 else 3, fontsize=fs,
              frameon=False, handlelength=2.0, columnspacing=1.2, borderaxespad=0.2)


def plate(p, nums=(), ghosts=(), stretch=None, window=(-8.5, 26.5), lateral="full", keys=None, width_in=8.3):
    """A concept plate: the call, the read and the progression, in one consistent style."""
    fld = draw(p, lateral=lateral, window=window, width_in=width_in)
    for pts in ghosts:
        ghost(fld, p, pts)
    for n, at in nums:
        num(fld, p, n, at)
    if stretch:
        tag(fld, p, stretch)
    field_legend(fld.ax, keys or PLATE_KEYS)
    return fld


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- frame strips (print) and video (web)
MARK_R = 0.7


def tracking(play):
    df = play.to_tracking()
    df["_id"] = df["displayName"].astype(str)
    return df


def frame_panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window_, rings=(), throw_t=None):
    """One moment of a simulated play, with faint trails, optional rings and the ball's flight so far."""
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    fid = int((tmap - t).abs().idxmin())
    ylo, yhi = sorted((play.ball_y - lateral[0], play.ball_y - lateral[1]))
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=play.los, window=window_, numbers=False, hashes=True,
                lateral=(ylo, yhi), to_go=play.to_go)
    cur = df[df["frameId"] == fid]
    shown = cur[cur["x"].between(play.los + window_[0] + 0.4, play.los + window_[1] - 0.4)
                & cur["y"].between(ylo + 0.4, yhi - 0.4)]
    ids = set(shown["_id"])
    trails = df[(df["frameId"] <= fid) & df["_id"].isin(ids) & (df["side"] != "ball")]
    for (_, side), g in trails.groupby(["_id", "side"]):
        xs, ys = fld.xy(g["x"].values, g["y"].values)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE if side == "off" else style.DEFENSE, lw=0.9, alpha=0.45, zorder=3)
    if throw_t is not None and t > throw_t:
        b = df[(df["side"] == "ball") & (df["frameId"] <= fid)]
        b = b[b["time"] >= throw_t - 0.05]
        xs, ys = fld.xy(b["x"].values, b["y"].values)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.BALL, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=9)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    for _, rr in shown.iterrows():
        x, y = (float(v) for v in fld.xy(rr["x"], rr["y"]))
        if rr["side"] == "ball":
            ax.add_patch(Ellipse((x, y), 1.0, 0.62, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.5, zorder=11))
            continue
        lab = str(rr.get("label", "") or "")
        if rr["side"] == "off":
            ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), MARK_R, fc=style.OFFENSE, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=8))
            tc = "white"
        else:
            ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=MARK_R * 1.3, orientation=np.pi / 4,
                                        fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT, ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0, zorder=8))
            tc = style.INK
        fs = max(4.0, min(8.0, ppy * (0.85 if len(lab) <= 1 else 0.62)))
        ax.text(x, y, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=tc, fontweight="bold", zorder=10)
    for key, col in rings:
        rr = cur[cur["displayName"] == key].iloc[0]
        x, y = fld.xy(rr["x"], rr["y"])
        ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), MARK_R * 1.6, fc="none", ec=col, lw=1.7, zorder=7))
    return fld


def strip(play, times, notes=None, lateral=(-24, 4), window=(-8, 14), ncols=2, rings=(), throw_t=None,
          width_in=6.5):
    df = tracking(play)
    nrows = int(np.ceil(len(times) / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    span_w, span_d = abs(lateral[1] - lateral[0]), window[1] - window[0]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, squeeze=False,
                             figsize=(width_in, nrows * (pw * span_d / span_w + (0.6 if notes else 0.25))))
    for ax in axes.flat[len(times):]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, t) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, times)):
        frame_panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings, throw_t)
        lab = "snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"{t:+.1f} s"
        ax.set_title(f"{i + 1}.  {lab}", fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK, loc="left")
        if notes:
            ax.text(0.5, -0.03, notes[i], transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=7.3,
                    color=style.INK, linespacing=1.2)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=2.2 if notes else 0.6, w_pad=0.6)
    return fig


def video(play, times, notes=None, lateral=(-24, 4), window=(-8, 14), rings=(), throw_t=None, width_in=5.6):
    from matplotlib import animation
    from IPython.display import HTML, display
    df = tracking(play)
    span_w, span_d = abs(lateral[1] - lateral[0]), window[1] - window[0]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(width_in, width_in * span_d / span_w + 0.4))
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()

    def update(fid):
        ax.clear()
        t = float(tmap[fid])
        frame_panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings, throw_t)
        txt = "snap" if abs(t) < 0.05 else f"{t:+.1f} s"
        if notes:
            cur = [n for tt, n in zip(times, notes) if tt <= t + 1e-6]
            txt += ("   " + cur[-1].replace("\n", " ")) if cur else ""
        ax.set_title(txt, fontsize=8, color=style.INK, loc="left")
        return []

    anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=sorted(df["frameId"].unique()), interval=100)
    html = (anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
            if shutil.which("ffmpeg") else anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once"))
    plt.close(fig)
    display(HTML(html))


def play_movie(play, times, notes=None, **kw):
    """Video on the website; a numbered, captioned frame strip in the PDF."""
    if PDF:
        strip(play, times, notes=notes, **kw)
        plt.show()
    else:
        kw.pop("ncols", None)
        kw.pop("width_in", None)
        video(play, times, notes=notes, **kw)


def set_track(p, key, rows, t_end=None):
    """Hand-made keyframes [(t, d, w), ...] for one player (gridiron's man() ends on top of the
    receiver, and we sometimes need a defender who detours around traffic). Call last."""
    kf, t0, t1 = p._compile()
    kf = dict(kf)
    q = p.players[key]
    rows = [(min(t0, -1.0), q.d, q.w), (0.0, q.d, q.w)] + [tuple(r_) for r_ in rows]
    kf[key] = np.array(rows, dtype=float)
    p._compiled = (kf, t0, max(t1, t_end or rows[-1][0]))


def chase(p, key, target, lag=0.3, off=(-1.0, 0.0), t_start=0.15, t_on=0.8, t_end=4.0, detour=None,
          lag_after=None):
    """Keyframes for a man defender trailing `target`: he starts where he is, then settles `off` =
    (down, toward the offense's right) yards from where the receiver was `lag` seconds earlier.
    detour = (t0, t1, (d, w)): between t0 and t1 he is pulled toward that point (traffic)."""
    q = p.players[key]
    rows = []
    for tt in np.round(np.arange(t_start, t_end, 0.05), 3):
        f = min(1.0, max(0.0, (tt - t_start) / (t_on - t_start)))
        f = f * f * (3 - 2 * f)
        lg = lag
        if detour is not None and lag_after is not None and tt > detour[0]:
            k = min(1.0, (tt - detour[0]) / (detour[1] - detour[0]))
            lg = lag + (lag_after - lag) * k
        tgt = p.position(target, max(0.0, tt - lg)) + np.array(off)
        pos = np.array([q.d, q.w]) * (1 - f) + tgt * f
        if detour is not None:
            a, b, pt = detour
            if a <= tt <= b:
                g = np.sin(np.pi * (tt - a) / (b - a))
                pos = pos * (1 - g) + np.array(pt) * g
        rows.append((tt, *pos))
    return rows


def catch_time(p):
    """Seconds after the snap at which the first pass arrives (rounded up to a tenth)."""
    for kind, to, te in p.ball_events:
        if kind == "pass":
            a, b = p.pass_target_spot()
            return float(np.ceil((te + np.hypot(*(b - a)) / gplay.BALL_SPEED) * 10) / 10)


@contextmanager
def ball_speed(v):
    """Temporarily change gridiron's ball speed (yd/s): a firm deep throw travels faster than the default."""
    old = gplay.BALL_SPEED
    gplay.BALL_SPEED = v
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        gplay.BALL_SPEED = old
```

Third-and-8, late in the first half. The offense lines up with two receivers on each side.
Before the snap the camera shows both safeties standing thirteen yards deep and both
cornerbacks only five yards off the ball, flat-footed, watching the quarterback. The ball is
snapped, the quarterback takes three quick steps back from the shotgun, and the outside
receiver on the right runs five yards and turns around. The cornerback in front of him does
exactly what he has been coached to do: he squats on that receiver. The ball sails over his
head to the inside receiver, who has run ten yards up the field and angled toward the
sideline, into the space behind the cornerback and in front of the safety. First down. On the
replay the analyst circles the two routes with his telestrator and says one word: *smash*. Why
was the cornerback wrong when he did what he was told? How did the quarterback know, before
the snap, where the ball was going? And why does the same two-route pattern, under one name or
another, show up in every playbook in the league? This chapter is about those patterns: the
**dropback concepts** that make up most of an offense's passing game beyond the quick throws.

**You'll be able to…**

- Say what a pass concept is, and why offenses teach concepts rather than individual routes.
- Draw fourteen dropback concepts (smash, flood, curl-flat, levels, drive, shallow cross,
  dagger, Y-cross, mesh, angle, four verticals, post-wheel, scissors and yankee) and point to
  the defender each one puts in a bind.
- Sort any concept into one of four families (vertical stretch, horizontal stretch, triangle,
  or man-beater) and name the coverage it is built to beat.
- Walk the quarterback's progression on each concept, from his first look to the checkdown.
- Spot a rub route on a replay and say where it crosses the line into an illegal pick.
- Explain tags and route conversions: how one call becomes the right answer against several
  coverages.

::: {.callout-note title="You'll need"}
- **Concepts, leverage and the pre-snap read** from [The Quick Game](04-03-quick-game.qmd):
  a concept puts two receivers on opposite sides of one defender; a defender's
  [leverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-leverage-inside-outside) (inside or outside the
  receiver) tells the quarterback where to throw; [stick](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-stick)
  and [snag](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-snag) are the short versions of ideas this chapter
  takes deeper.
- **Routes, drops and reads** from [Passing Fundamentals](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd): the
  route tree ([hitch](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hitch), [curl](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-curl-route),
  [dig](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-dig), [corner](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-corner-route),
  [post](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-post), [go](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-go-route),
  [seam](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-seam), [wheel](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-wheel));
  the [progression](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-progression), the order in which the
  quarterback looks at his receivers; the [high-low](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-high-low-read)
  and [horizontal](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-horizontal-stretch) stretches of a
  [conflict defender](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-conflict-defender); and the
  [option route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-option-route).
- **Man, zone and the shell** from [A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd):
  in man coverage each defender follows a receiver, in zone each guards an area;
  [one-high](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-one-high) means one deep safety in the middle,
  [two-high](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-two-high) means two.
- **Protection** from [Pass Protection](04-02-pass-protection.qmd): deeper throws need the line
  (and sometimes a back and a tight end) to hold up for three seconds or more.
:::

## What a pass concept is

A [**pass concept**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pass-concept) is a set of routes designed
to work together on one play, usually by putting one or two defenders in a position where
whatever they do leaves a receiver open. You met the idea in
[The Quick Game](04-03-quick-game.qmd), where slant-flat and stick each pinned one defender
between two receivers. This chapter takes the same idea deeper down the field, where the
routes take longer to develop and the defenders in conflict are cornerbacks, linebackers and
safeties instead of a single slot defender.

Why do offenses think in concepts rather than routes? Three reasons, and they explain a lot
about how football is coached.

**A concept is a sentence; routes are only words.** A corner route on its own means nothing.
A corner route run over a hitch, against a cornerback who has to choose between them, is a
plan. The quarterback doesn't read five receivers one by one; he reads one or two defenders
and lets the concept tell him where the open man will be. That's why concepts are drawn and
taught as units, and why a receiver learns not only his route but his partner's.

**A name is a shortcut.** "Smash" tells two receivers their routes in one syllable, from any
formation, on either side of the field. Offenses that name concepts this way can teach a
playbook faster and call plays faster, which matters in a two-minute drive or a no-huddle
attack. Not every system names its plays like this; some spell out each receiver's route in
a long string of words or numbers, and the trade-offs between those styles are the subject of
[Offensive Systems and Languages](04-08-offensive-systems-and-languages.qmd), where
[concept-based terminology](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-concept-based-terminology) gets
its full story.

**A concept travels.** Smash works from a 2x2 formation, from trips, with a tight end as the
inside receiver or a running back. Because the conflict is about *space* (the gap between a
cornerback sitting short and a safety playing deep), the same concept can be dressed up in a
dozen formations, which makes it hard for a defense to recognize from the alignment alone.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Every pass play has one intended receiver." Almost none do. A concept has a *first look*, the
route it was designed around, but it's built so that whichever choice the key defender makes,
somebody else is open. When an announcer says the quarterback "went to his second read," that
isn't a failure of the play. It is often the play working as drawn.
:::

### What changes when the quarterback drops back

The quick game lives on throws that leave the quarterback's hand in about two seconds, aimed
at receivers five or six yards away. Dropback concepts give themselves more time and aim
farther, and the numbers show what that buys and what it costs. In the 2025 regular season,
throws that traveled less than ten yards past the line of scrimmage left the quarterback's
hand after a median of 2.3 seconds; throws of 10 to 19 yards, the home of most of the concepts
in this chapter, took 2.8 seconds, and throws of 20 yards or more took 3.1 seconds.[^ttt] That
extra half-second is the price of the deeper drop (five steps from under center, or three from
the shotgun, in the matched pairs of [Passing Fundamentals](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd)) and
of routes that need ten or fifteen yards to reach the spot where they break.

What does the half-second buy? Value. Those 10-to-19-yard throws averaged about +0.39
[expected points added](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-epa) (EPA) per attempt, the course's
measure of how much a play changed the offense's scoring chances, against about +0.10 for throws
under ten yards. But they were completed only 54% of the time, against 72%, and they were
intercepted twice as often (about 3.2% of attempts against 1.6%).

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists, and what it costs"}
Dropback concepts trade **time and risk for yards**. The offense asks its line to protect for
three seconds or more, accepts a lower completion rate and more interceptions, and gets in
return the throws that move the ball in big pieces: the 15-yard dig on third-and-8, the corner
route that turns a drive into a scoring chance. The quick game keeps an offense on schedule;
dropback concepts are how it gets ahead of it. The bill comes in sacks, hits on the quarterback
and a pass rush with time to get home, which is why protection
([Pass Protection](04-02-pass-protection.qmd)) and dropback concepts are planned together.
:::

## Four ways to put a defender in a bind

Every concept in this chapter does one of four things to the defense. Learn the four and you
can name the purpose of a concept you have never seen, which is most of what "reading" a pass
play from the couch means.

```{python}
#| label: fig-families
#| fig-cap: "The four families of pass concepts, drawn as small abstract pictures (offense moving up the page). 1. Vertical stretch (high-low): two receivers in one defender's area at two depths; he can stand under the high one or in front of the low one, not both. 2. Horizontal stretch: receivers on both sides of a defender at about the same depth. 3. Triangle: three receivers around two defenders, one high and two low, so the quarterback has a high-low and an inside-outside choice at once. 4. Man-beater: against man coverage there is no area to overload, so the routes cross close to each other and the defenders chasing them have to fight through traffic (the dotted orange line is a defender forced to go around)."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.5, 5.0))
# 1 vertical
p1 = Play([O("A", "WR", 0.0, -2.0, "A"), O("B", "WR", 0.0, 2.0, "B")],
          [D("D1", "LB", 6.5, 0.0, "D")], los=LOS, to_go=None)
route_to(p1, "A", (5.0, -2.0), (11.5, -0.6))
route_to(p1, "B", (1.0, 2.0), (2.2, 0.4))
p1.highlight("D1")
# 2 horizontal
p2 = Play([O("A", "WR", 0.0, -7.0, "A"), O("B", "WR", 0.0, 7.0, "B")],
          [D("D1", "LB", 6.0, 0.0, "D")], los=LOS, to_go=None)
route_to(p2, "A", (5.5, -7.0), (6.0, -4.8))
route_to(p2, "B", (5.5, 7.0), (6.0, 4.8))
p2.highlight("D1")
# 3 triangle
p3 = Play([O("A", "WR", 0.0, 7.5, "A"), O("B", "WR", 0.0, 3.0, "B"), O("C", "RB", -2.0, -2.0, "C")],
          [D("D1", "LB", 6.0, 5.5, "D"), D("D2", "LB", 6.0, -2.5, "D")], los=LOS, to_go=None)
route_to(p3, "A", (11.0, 7.5), (10.0, 6.4))
route_to(p3, "B", (1.5, 5.5), (2.5, 9.8))
route_to(p3, "C", (-1.0, 0.0), (4.0, 1.4))
p3.highlight("D1", "D2")
# 4 man-beater
p4 = Play([O("A", "WR", 0.0, -6.0, "A"), O("B", "WR", 0.0, 6.0, "B")],
          [D("D1", "CB", 1.4, -5.6, "D"), D("D2", "CB", 1.4, 5.6, "D")], los=LOS, to_go=None)
route_to(p4, "A", (5.0, -5.6), (6.5, 6.5))
route_to(p4, "B", (4.0, 5.6), (5.0, -6.5))
for ax, (p, ttl) in zip(axes.flat, ((p1, "1. Vertical stretch (high-low)"), (p2, "2. Horizontal stretch"),
                                    (p3, "3. Triangle"), (p4, "4. Man-beater"))):
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-11.5, 11.5), window=(-3.5, 14.5), show_ruler=False, width_in=3.2)
    panel_title(ax, ttl, fs=8.5)
    if p is p1:
        opening(fld, p, (11.0, -0.6), (2.2, 3.2))
        opening(fld, p, (2.3, 0.4), (2.0, 3.2))
        say(fld, p, 11.6, 5.4, "high", color=OD)
        say(fld, p, 2.3, 4.6, "low", color=OD)
        say(fld, p, 6.5, -5.4, "one defender,\ntwo depths", color=DD)
    elif p is p2:
        say(fld, p, 9.0, 0.0, "one defender,\ntwo sides", color=DD)
        say(fld, p, 2.4, -4.5, "inside", color=OD)
        say(fld, p, 2.4, 4.5, "outside", color=OD)
    elif p is p3:
        triangle(fld, p, [(10.0, 6.4), (2.5, 9.8), (4.0, 1.4)])
        say(fld, p, 12.4, -3.0, "two defenders,\nthree receivers", color=DD)
    else:
        branch(fld, p, [(1.4, -5.6), (4.0, -4.6), (4.4, -1.6), (2.6, 0.2), (4.0, 2.6), (5.2, 4.4)],
               color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4, dash=(0, (1, 1.6)))
        say(fld, p, 11.0, 0.0, "B's path is in the way:\nA's defender has to\ngo around (dotted)", color=DD)

```

1. **Vertical stretch (high-low).** Two receivers in one defender's area, one above him and
   one below. He can sink under the high route or come up on the low one, not both. This is the
   [high-low read](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-high-low-read) of
   [Passing Fundamentals](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd), and it is the most common family by
   far: smash, flood, levels, drive, shallow cross, dagger, Y-cross and yankee are all built on
   it.
2. **Horizontal stretch.** Receivers on both sides of a defender at about the same depth, the
   [horizontal stretch](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-horizontal-stretch) of Passing
   Fundamentals. Underneath, that's the quick game's spacing; deep, it is four verticals,
   post-wheel and scissors, which stretch the *deep* defenders side to side.
3. **Triangle.** Three receivers arranged around two defenders. A
   [**triangle read**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-triangle-read) is a three-receiver read
   in which the routes form a triangle, one high and two low (or two high and one low), so the
   quarterback has a high-low *and* an inside-outside choice at once. Snag, from the quick game,
   is the classic; curl-flat with a third route inside is the dropback version.
4. **Man-beater.** A [**man-beater**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-man-beater) is a concept
   designed to beat man coverage. Stretches beat zone defenders, who guard areas; a man defender
   follows one receiver wherever he goes, so there is no area to overload. Man-beaters win
   instead with routes that cross close together (so defenders run into traffic), routes that
   break away from a defender's leverage, and mismatches like a running back against a
   linebacker. Mesh and the angle route are the classics.

Most real concepts are hybrids (a flood is a vertical stretch that also stretches the flat
defender sideways; mesh sits in zone holes when it isn't running away from man defenders), so
the family names describe a concept's *main* idea. That idea also tells you what coverage the
concept is built to beat, and therefore when an offense will call it. We'll come back to that
matchup at the end of the chapter, and [What Beats What](../08-the-chess-match/08-01-concepts-versus-coverages.qmd)
builds it into a full table.

### How to read the plates

The fourteen concepts below are drawn as *plates*, the way a playbook draws them, in one
consistent style:

- The offense is in shotgun with 11 personnel (one back, one tight end, three receivers) unless
  the caption says otherwise: **X** and **Z** are the outside receivers, **H** a slot receiver,
  **Y** a tight end or second slot, **R** the running back. The ball is in the middle of the
  field to keep the picture symmetric; in a game, most concepts are aimed at the wide side.
- Blue routes are the concept. **Grey** routes are part of the call but outside the read: they
  are there to hold defenders in place.
- **Green numbers** are the progression, the order in which the quarterback looks. These are
  typical teaching orders; every team writes its own, and many change the order by coverage.
- The defense is drawn in the coverage the concept is built to beat. Dashed orange arrows are
  zone drops; the **ringed** defender is the one in conflict, the man the quarterback reads.
- The label at the top right names the concept's family.

## Vertical stretches on the sideline: smash, flood and curl-flat

The first three concepts attack the area near one sideline, where a defense has only two or
three defenders and the sideline itself acts as a twelfth defender for the offense: a receiver
running toward it has somewhere to go, and the defender has to cover him all the way there.

### Smash: the corner over the hitch

[**Smash**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-smash) pairs two receivers on one side. The outside
receiver runs a hitch at five or six yards and turns back to the quarterback. The inside receiver
runs a corner route: ten or twelve yards straight up the field, then an angle toward the sideline
and the back of the end zone. The defender in conflict is the cornerback on that side.

```{python}
#| label: fig-smash
#| fig-cap: "Smash to the offense's right against Cover 2. Z runs a hitch at five yards; Y, from the slot, runs a corner route over him, flattening toward the sideline at about 16 yards. The ringed cornerback squats in the flat, as Cover 2 tells him to, and the strong safety (SS) has the deep half behind him, starting thirteen yards deep and well inside him: the corner route lands in the gap between them (green). The progression reads the cornerback high to low: (1) the corner route if he sits on the hitch, (2) the hitch if he sinks under the corner route, (3) the back as the checkdown. The left side (grey) is often a mirror-image smash, so the quarterback can pick the side he likes before the snap."
p = Play(spread(), cover2(), los=LOS, to_go=8)
protect(p)
p.dropback(2.5)
p.route("Z", r.hitch(5.0))
route_to(p, "Y", (8.5, 9.0), (16.0, 17.5))
rb_n = swing(p, -1)
p.drop("RCB", (6.0, 17.2))
p.drop("SS", (18.5, 11.5))
p.drop("NB", (8.5, 8.4))
p.drop("MIKE", (9.0, 1.2))
p.drop("WILL", (8.5, -8.0))
p.drop("FS", (18.5, -11.5))
p.drop("LCB", (6.0, -17.2))
p.highlight("RCB")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (17.6, 20.0)), (2, (6.4, 13.0)), (3, rb_n)],
            ghosts=[[(-0.7, -15.0), (5.3, -15.0), (4.3, -14.4)], [(-1.5, -9.0), (8.5, -9.0), (16.0, -17.5)]],
            stretch="Vertical stretch: the cornerback")
opening(fld, p, (14.0, 17.0), (4.6, 5.6))
point_to(fld, p, (21.0, 1.0), (15.0, 15.0), "corner route lands\nbehind the CB, in front\nof the safety",
         color=READ_GREEN)
say(fld, p, 2.6, 21.6, "CB squats\non the hitch", color=DD)
plt.show()
```

Why does it work against [Cover 2](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-2)? Cover 2 splits the
deep field between two safeties and asks the cornerbacks to stay short, guarding the flats, so
that nothing quick gets thrown to the outside. That leaves a seam of open grass along each
sideline between the corner's short zone and the safety's deep half, roughly 12 to 20 yards
deep, and the safety has to cover it from his spot near the hash, ten or fifteen yards away. The corner route aims at
that seam. If the cornerback stays on the hitch, which is his job, the corner route is open
behind him. If he gives ground to take away the corner route, the hitch is open in front of him.
Either way the quarterback only has to watch one man.

The corner route has to be thrown with care. Too flat and the cornerback can recover under it;
too high and the safety arrives. Many teams build a rule into the route (a
[route conversion](#tags-and-route-conversions), which we'll get to): against two deep safeties,
flatten it and stay under the safety; against one deep safety, push it deeper toward the pylon.

**What smash gives up.** Against [Cover 3](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-3), whose
cornerbacks drop into deep thirds instead of squatting, the corner route runs into a defender
standing right on top of it, so the read flips: the cornerback bails, and the hitch underneath is
the throw. Against man coverage, smash becomes two one-on-one routes, a hitch that has to beat a
cornerback and a corner route that has to beat a slot defender, which is fine if the receivers
are better than the defenders and not otherwise. Smash is a Cover 2 beater first, a decent
answer to Cover 3 second, and only a hope against man.

### Flood: three levels on one sideline

[**Flood**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-flood) (many teams call it
[**sail**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-sail)) puts three receivers at three depths near
one sideline: one deep, one in between and one shallow. On the strong side of a
Cover 3 defense there are only two defenders in that area, the cornerback, who has the deep
third, and the curl-flat defender underneath. Three receivers, two defenders.

```{python}
#| label: fig-flood
#| fig-cap: "Flood to the offense's right against Cover 3. Z runs a go route that carries the cornerback deep (the clear-out). Y runs a sail route: ten yards up the seam, then an angle toward the sideline that settles at about 13 yards. The back runs to the flat. The ringed nickel ($) is the curl-flat defender, the man in conflict: (1) the sail if he comes up to the flat, (2) the flat if he sinks under the sail. The go route isn't in the progression unless the cornerback lets Z run past him. On the left, X and H run routes that keep the linebacker and the free safety from drifting over."
p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.5), cover3(nb_side=1), los=LOS, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(2.5)
p.route("Z", r.go(23.0))
route_to(p, "Y", (8.5, 9.0), (13.0, 17.8))
route_to(p, "RB", (-3.6, 5.0), (1.0, 11.5), (2.4, 16.5))
p.drop("RCB", (17.0, 16.6))
p.drop("NB", (8.0, 12.5))
p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, 3.0))
p.drop("FS", (17.0, 0.0))
p.drop("WILL", (8.0, -4.0))
p.drop("SS", (7.0, -12.0))
p.drop("LCB", (17.0, -16.6))
p.highlight("NB")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (13.0, 20.3)), (2, (2.4, 19.2))],
            ghosts=[[(-0.7, -15.0), (11.3, -15.0), (10.0, -13.8)], [(-1.5, -9.0), (20.0, -7.6)]],
            stretch="Vertical stretch: three levels")
say(fld, p, 19.5, 10.5, "go: clears\nthe corner", color=OD)
say(fld, p, 9.6, 21.7, "sail", color=OD)
say(fld, p, -1.4, 21.3, "flat", color=OD)
plt.show()
```

Flood is a vertical stretch with three floors instead of two. The go route occupies the top
floor and takes the cornerback with it, because a Cover 3 cornerback is taught never to let
anyone get behind him. That leaves the curl-flat defender alone with the sail and the flat, the
same high-low you saw in curl-flat and slant-flat, but with the high route farther outside and
deeper, where it is harder to reach. If the curl-flat defender takes the flat, the sail settles
in the space he left, in front of the cornerback, for 12 or 14 yards. If he sinks, the back
catches the ball in the flat with open grass in front of him.

Flood's cost is the other side of the field. It sends three receivers to one sideline, so the
backside routes are usually just there to hold defenders, and a defense that rotates its
coverage toward the flood (a safety rolling down to the flat side at the snap) can outnumber
it. That is why flood is so often run off a fake run or with the quarterback rolling toward
the flood side; the run fake and the bootleg, which move the defenders before the routes even
arrive, are in [Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens](04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd).

### Curl-flat: the West Coast triangle

[**Curl-flat**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-curl-flat) is the high-low you met in
[Passing Fundamentals](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd): a curl at 10 to 12 yards over a flat
route underneath, both in the area of the one defender who guards the short outside zone. As
a dropback concept it usually comes with a third route, a back or tight end who settles in a
hook route just inside the curl at five or six yards. That third route turns a two-man read into
a triangle.

```{python}
#| label: fig-curl-flat
#| fig-cap: "Curl-flat to the offense's right, with the back's hook route inside, against Cover 3. Z runs a curl at 12 yards, Y runs to the flat, and the back checks for a blitzer, then settles at five yards over the right tackle. The three routes form a triangle (shaded) around two defenders: the ringed nickel ($), who guards the curl-flat area, and the Mike (M), who guards the hook. The progression: (1) the curl, if the $ widens to the flat; (2) the flat, if he sinks under the curl; (3) the hook, if both of them get width or depth. The left side runs a mirror-image curl and a seam (grey)."
p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.5), cover3(nb_side=1), los=LOS, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(2.5)
p.route("Z", r.curl(12.0))
route_to(p, "Y", (1.0, 11.5), (2.0, 17.5))
route_to(p, "RB", (-3.5, 3.8), (4.5, 4.6), (4.3, 3.8))
p.drop("NB", (8.5, 11.0))
p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, 2.4))
p.drop("RCB", (17.0, 16.6))
p.drop("FS", (17.0, 0.0))
p.drop("WILL", (8.0, -4.0))
p.drop("SS", (7.0, -12.0))
p.drop("LCB", (17.0, -16.6))
p.highlight("NB", "MIKE")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (12.8, 12.6)), (2, (4.4, 19.4)), (3, (6.4, 4.4))],
            ghosts=[[(-0.7, -15.0), (11.3, -15.0), (9.8, -13.8)], [(-1.5, -9.0), (20.0, -7.6)]],
            stretch="Triangle: the $ and the Mike")
triangle(fld, p, [(9.8, 13.8), (2.0, 17.5), (4.3, 3.8)])
plt.show()
```

The triangle is what makes the concept durable. The nickel can't cover the curl and the flat
(that's the high-low), and if he splits the difference, the Mike has to choose between helping
on the curl and standing on the hook (that's the in-out). The quarterback reads it with the
same rhythm on almost every snap: eyes to the curl as his back foot lands, then down to the
flat, then inside to the hook. The routes are short enough that the ball comes out in under
three seconds, which is why curl-flat sits at the border between the quick game and the
dropback game.

Curl-flat is a [West Coast](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-west-coast-offense) staple, the
family of offenses descended from Bill Walsh's 49ers, which were built on high-percentage
throws with a third receiver underneath as the safety valve. Its weakness is its depth. Every
route in the triangle is within 12 yards of the line of scrimmage, so a defense that squeezes
the short zones and tackles well can hold it to a five-yard gain; and against two-high
coverages, whose cornerbacks often sit short and outside, the curl can find a defender standing
right on top of it.

## Vertical stretches in the middle: levels, drive, shallow cross and dagger

The next four concepts carry the high-low into the middle of the field, where the linebackers
live. The middle is harder to throw into (there are more defenders there, and they are closer
together) but it's also the most valuable area on the field, as the chart at the end of this
section shows. The defender in conflict in each of these concepts is a linebacker, or a safety
standing behind the linebackers, and the routes are mostly in-breakers: digs, shallow crosses
and in routes that run across his face.

### Levels: two in-breakers, two depths

[**Levels**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-levels) sends two receivers from the same side
across the field on in-breaking routes at two depths: in the most common version the outside
receiver runs a short in at about five yards and the inside receiver a dig at about twelve. The defender between those levels is the
linebacker guarding the hook area on that side.

```{python}
#| label: fig-levels
#| fig-cap: "Levels to the offense's left against Cover 3. H, from the slot, runs a dig at 12 yards; X, from outside, runs a short in route at about 4 yards underneath him. The ringed Will linebacker (W), who drops to the hook area on that side, is the man in conflict: (1) the dig if he jumps the short in route; (2) the in route if he drops under the dig; (3) the back, who checks for a blitzer, then releases to the flat on the right. On the right, Y's seam and Z's go route (grey) keep the free safety in the middle and the cornerback deep."
p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.5), cover3(nb_side=-1), los=LOS, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(2.5)
p.route("H", r.dig(13.0, 12.0))
route_to(p, "X", (3.2, -15.0), (3.6, -5.0))
rb_n = swing(p, 1)
p.drop("WILL", (7.5, -6.5))
p.drop("NB", (7.0, -12.0))
p.drop("MIKE", (7.5, 3.5))
p.drop("SS", (7.0, 11.5))
p.drop("LCB", (17.0, -16.6))
p.drop("RCB", (17.0, 16.6))
p.drop("FS", (17.0, 0.0))
p.highlight("WILL")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (12.4, 5.6)), (2, (1.4, -12.2)), (3, rb_n)],
            ghosts=[[(-1.5, 9.0), (20.0, 7.6)], [(-0.7, 15.0), (21.0, 15.0)]],
            stretch="Vertical stretch: the hook linebacker")
say(fld, p, 14.6, -9.0, "dig (high)", color=OD)
say(fld, p, 2.0, -20.0, "in (low)", color=OD)
plt.show()
```

Why in-breakers? Because the linebacker in the middle is usually watching the quarterback, not
the receivers, and he drops *backward*, which makes him slow to react to a route crossing in front
of him or behind him. The short in route arrives first; the dig arrives a beat later, behind him.
Coaches teach the quarterback to look high first: if the linebacker comes up on the in route,
the dig behind him is the bigger gain. Peyton Manning's Indianapolis offenses (where the play was
called "Dig") ran levels so often, by Chris Brown's count, that ten times a game was not unusual,
and its logic, two in-breakers on two floors, runs through many of the
middle-of-the-field concepts that follow.[^colts]

### Drive: the shallow and the dig, together

[**Drive**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-drive-concept) is levels stretched across the whole
field. One receiver runs a shallow cross, two to four yards deep, all the way to the far side;
a teammate from the same side runs a dig at about twelve yards behind him, following him
across. The pair passes through the hook zones of both linebackers.

```{python}
#| label: fig-drive
#| fig-cap: "Drive against Cover 3. From the right, Y runs a shallow cross at about three yards all the way across the formation; Z runs a 12-yard dig behind him on the same path. The ringed Mike (M) can step up to the shallow or sink under the dig, not both: (1) the shallow, if he drops; (2) the dig, if he comes up; (3) the back, who checks for a blitzer and releases to the left. X's go route and H's seam (grey) take the left cornerback and the free safety deep, clearing the area where both crossers finish."
p = Play(spread(), cover3(nb_side=1), los=LOS, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(2.5)
route_to(p, "Y", (1.0, 7.5), (2.8, -13.0))
p.route("Z", r.dig(12.0, 24.0))
rb_n = swing(p, -1)
p.drop("MIKE", (7.0, 2.0))
p.drop("WILL", (7.0, -4.5))
p.drop("NB", (7.0, 12.0))
p.drop("SS", (7.0, -12.0))
p.drop("LCB", (17.0, -16.6))
p.drop("RCB", (17.0, 16.6))
p.drop("FS", (17.0, 0.0))
p.highlight("MIKE")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (4.6, -12.6)), (2, (13.2, -11.0)), (3, rb_n)],
            ghosts=[[(-0.7, -15.0), (21.0, -15.0)], [(-1.5, -9.0), (20.0, -7.6)]],
            stretch="Vertical stretch: the Mike")
say(fld, p, 0.8, 21.5, "shallow at 2-4 yd", color=OD)
say(fld, p, 9.5, 21.0, "dig at 12 yd", color=OD)
plt.show()
```

The shallow cross is the engine. A receiver crossing the field at three yards is a nightmare
in man coverage, because his defender has to chase him through the traffic of linemen and
linebackers and can never get in front of him; against zone, he runs through one hook defender
after another, and each one has to decide whether to come up and take him. The moment one does,
the dig is open behind. That makes drive one of the most useful concepts in football: a man-beater
and a zone-beater in the same call. Drive is in a great many NFL playbooks, often under that name,
and it's a favorite of offenses that like to make the defense tackle a receiver who catches the
ball running full speed across the field.

### Shallow cross: the Air Raid's bread and butter

[**Shallow cross**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-shallow-cross) uses the same two routes as
drive, a shallow cross under a deeper in-breaker, but sends them from *opposite* sides. One
receiver runs the shallow at four or five yards; the receiver from the other side runs a dig or a
"sit" route at 10 to 12 yards, settling over the ball. The two routes cross the middle of the
field going in opposite directions, so the middle linebacker has a receiver coming from each
side at once.

```{python}
#| label: fig-shallow
#| fig-cap: "Shallow cross against Cover 2. From the right, Z runs a shallow cross at about four yards to the left; from the left, H runs a dig that settles at 11 yards over the ball. The ringed Mike (M), dropping into the middle, is the read: (1) the shallow, if he sinks; (2) the dig, if he comes up for the shallow; (3) the back on the left as the checkdown. X and Y (grey) run vertically to hold the two safeties, so nobody sinks under the dig from above. Against man coverage, the shallow simply runs away from his defender, and the two crossing paths add traffic."
p = Play(spread(), cover2(), los=LOS, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(2.5)
route_to(p, "Z", (2.0, 13.0), (3.6, 9.0), (3.6, -12.0))
route_to(p, "H", (8.0, -9.0), (11.0, -6.5), (11.0, 2.0))
rb_n = swing(p, -1)
p.drop("MIKE", (9.5, 0.0))
p.drop("WILL", (8.5, -8.0))
p.drop("NB", (8.5, 8.4))
p.drop("LCB", (6.0, -17.2))
p.drop("RCB", (6.0, 17.2))
p.drop("FS", (18.5, -11.5))
p.drop("SS", (18.5, 11.5))
p.highlight("MIKE")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (5.4, -13.6)), (2, (12.6, 3.6)), (3, rb_n)],
            ghosts=[[(-0.7, -15.0), (21.0, -15.0)], [(-1.5, 9.0), (21.0, 7.5)]],
            stretch="Vertical stretch: the Mike")
say(fld, p, 3.4, 19.0, "shallow at 4-5 yd", color=OD)
say(fld, p, 13.0, -14.2, "dig or sit at 11 yd", color=OD)
plt.show()
```

The shallow cross is the play most associated with the
[Air Raid](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-air-raid), the pass-first college offense built by
Hal Mumme and Mike Leach (its story is below), which ran it with wide line splits and a
quarterback taught to throw the shallow the instant the linebacker dropped. It works for the same
reason drive does, plus one more: because the two crossers come from opposite sides, a man
defender chasing the shallow may have to run around the dig receiver coming the other way. That
is the first appearance of an idea we'll make explicit with mesh, the rub.

### Dagger: clear the seam, fill it behind

[**Dagger**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-dagger) is the deep member of the family, and the
one built to beat two-high coverages. The inside receiver runs straight up the seam; the outside
receiver runs a deep dig, 15 to 18 yards, coming in behind him.

```{python}
#| label: fig-dagger
#| fig-cap: "Dagger to the offense's right against Quarters. Y runs straight up the seam; Z runs a dig at about 15 yards, in behind him. The ringed strong safety (SS) is reading Y, the second receiver from the sideline, as Quarters tells him to, so the seam pulls him deep, and the nickel and Mike sink with it; the dig arrives in the space they vacate, under the safeties and over the linebackers. The progression: (1) the seam, if the safety doesn't carry it; (2) the dig; (3) the back, the checkdown on the left. On the left, X and H run routes (grey) that keep the free safety from drifting over."
p = Play(spread(), quarters(), los=LOS, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(3.0)
p.route("Y", r.seam(24.0))
p.route("Z", r.dig(15.5, 19.0))
rb_n = swing(p, -1)
p.drop("SS", (19.0, 9.0))
p.drop("RCB", (17.5, 16.0))
p.drop("NB", (11.0, 8.6))
p.drop("MIKE", (9.0, 3.0))
p.drop("WILL", (8.5, -7.0))
p.drop("FS", (13.0, -11.0))
p.drop("LCB", (16.0, -16.6))
p.highlight("SS")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (21.0, 10.6)), (2, (16.6, -5.8)), (3, rb_n)],
            ghosts=[[(-0.7, -15.0), (11.3, -15.0), (9.8, -13.8)], [(-1.5, -9.0), (5.0, -9.0), (5.2, -7.0)]],
            stretch="Vertical stretch: safety and linebackers")
opening(fld, p, (14.8, -1.0), (4.0, 9.0))
say(fld, p, 22.6, 4.0, "the seam pulls\nthem deep", color=OD)
say(fld, p, 11.8, -1.0, "dig fills in\nbehind them", color=READ_GREEN, weight="bold")
plt.show()
```

Why would two-high coverages be vulnerable to this? In
[Quarters](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-quarters) and its relatives, each safety reads the
inside receiver on his side: if that receiver goes vertical, the safety takes him deep. That rule
is what makes Quarters so good against the run and the quick game, because the safety can come
up hard on anything short. Dagger turns the rule against him. The seam pulls the safety deep and
drags the underneath defenders back with it, and the dig, timed to arrive a beat later, settles in
the empty middle between the levels. Against one-high coverage the read is similar but the
threat is different: the seam attacks the single safety, and if he stays in the middle, the dig
crosses under him. Dagger needs time, because a 16-yard dig takes a deep drop and three seconds
or more, which is why it's usually called with six- or seven-man protection.

### Where the value is

Why do offenses work so hard to throw into the middle, where the linebackers are, rather than
to the open sideline? The chart answers that with three seasons of throws.

```{python}
#| label: fig-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Expected points added (EPA) per pass attempt by where the ball was thrown, 2023–2025 regular seasons: rows are depth past the line of scrimmage (air yards), columns are the play-by-play charter's left, middle and right thirds of the field. Blue cells added value on average, red cells lost it; the small number is the count of attempts. The intermediate middle (10–20 yards between the hashes, where levels, drive, shallow cross, dagger and Y-cross throw) is the most valuable area on the field per attempt, worth half a point or more. Deep throws are valuable everywhere but rarer; throws behind the line lose value on average. Sacks and spikes are excluded; interceptions count against the cell they were thrown to."
order = ["30+", "20–29", "15–19", "10–14", "5–9", "0–4", "behind"]
bins = [-99, 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 99]
labs = ["behind", "0–4", "5–9", "10–14", "15–19", "20–29", "30+"]
h = ATT.copy()
h["depth"] = pd.cut(h["air_yards"], bins, labels=labs, right=False)
g = h.groupby(["depth", "pass_location"], observed=True)["epa"].agg(["mean", "size"]).reset_index()
M = g.pivot(index="depth", columns="pass_location", values="mean").loc[order, ["left", "middle", "right"]]
N = g.pivot(index="depth", columns="pass_location", values="size").loc[order, ["left", "middle", "right"]]
from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap, TwoSlopeNorm
cmap = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("div", [style.DIVERGING[2], style.DIVERGING[1], style.DIVERGING[0]])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 4.0))
ax.imshow(M.values, cmap=cmap, norm=TwoSlopeNorm(vmin=-0.6, vcenter=0.0, vmax=0.6), aspect="auto")
for i in range(M.shape[0]):
    for j in range(M.shape[1]):
        v = M.values[i, j]
        ax.text(j, i - 0.08, f"{v:+.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9.5,
                color="white" if abs(v) > 0.42 else style.INK, fontweight="bold")
        ax.text(j, i + 0.26, f"n = {int(N.values[i, j]):,}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.6,
                color="white" if abs(v) > 0.42 else style.INK_2)
ax.set_xticks(range(3), ["left third", "middle", "right third"], fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(order)), [f"{o} yd" if o != "behind" else "behind LOS" for o in order], fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Where the ball went (offense's view)", fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_ylabel("Air yards", fontsize=8.5)
ax.grid(False)
for sp in ax.spines.values():
    sp.set_visible(False)
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((0.5, 1.5), 1.0, 2.0, fill=False, ec=style.INK, lw=1.6, zorder=5))
ax.set_title("EPA per attempt by depth and direction, 2023–2025", fontsize=9.5, loc="left")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The boxed cells are the payoff. Over three seasons, a throw of 10 to 19 yards into the middle of
the field added about half an expected point on average, more than the same depth toward either
sideline and more than any short throw anywhere.[^heat] Two cautions keep the chart honest.
First, it shows where the ball *went*, not where the quarterback *wanted* it to go: quarterbacks
throw into the middle when somebody is open there, so the cells partly measure good decisions.
Second, the middle is also where interceptions happen (the defenders are closer together), and
those are already folded into the averages. Even so, the shape explains a great deal of offensive
design: the intermediate middle is worth fighting for, and the concepts in this section are the
tools for getting there.

## Y-cross: a flood built from across the field

[**Y-cross**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-y-cross) combines the two ideas so far, the
three-level flood and the in-breaker through the middle. A receiver from one side (in the Air
Raid's lettering, the Y, the inside receiver) runs a crossing route that climbs to 15 or 18
yards as it goes and finishes near the far sideline. On that far side, the outside receiver runs
a go route to clear the cornerback away and another receiver runs to the flat. The result is a
flood whose middle level arrives from the other side of the field, at full speed, where no
defender on that side was looking for it.

```{python}
#| label: fig-y-cross
#| fig-cap: "Y-cross against Cover 3. Y, from the right slot, crosses the field, climbing to about 15 yards at the far numbers. On the left, X runs a go route that takes the cornerback deep and H runs to the flat underneath. Z's post (grey) holds the free safety in the middle. The ringed strong safety, the curl-flat defender on the left, faces a high-low: (1) the cross if he comes up to the flat; (2) the flat if he sinks under the cross; (3) the back, who checks for a blitzer, then swings to the right. Teams usually run it toward the wide side of the field, so the crosser has room to finish."
p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.5), cover3(nb_side=1), los=LOS, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(3.0)
route_to(p, "Y", (3.5, 8.0), (11.5, -1.0), (14.5, -15.0))
p.route("X", r.go(23.0))
route_to(p, "H", (0.5, -11.5), (2.0, -17.0))
rb_n = swing(p, 1)
p.drop("SS", (8.0, -12.0))
p.drop("LCB", (17.0, -16.6))
p.drop("FS", (17.0, 0.0))
p.drop("WILL", (8.0, -4.0))
p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, 3.0))
p.drop("NB", (8.0, 12.0))
p.drop("RCB", (17.0, 16.6))
p.highlight("SS")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (16.4, -13.0)), (2, (3.6, -19.6)), (3, rb_n)],
            ghosts=[[(-0.7, 15.0), (11.3, 15.0), (21.0, 8.0)]],
            stretch="Vertical stretch: three levels")
say(fld, p, 23.8, -11.6, "go: clears\nthe corner", color=OD)
say(fld, p, 17.8, -6.5, "the cross\nclimbs to 15", color=OD)
plt.show()
```

The quarterback reads Y-cross like a flood: eyes on the curl-flat defender on the far side,
cross over flat. What makes it special is timing and angle. The crosser is running away from the
defenders who started on his side and toward a defender who has to turn and find him, so he
arrives in the window with momentum and with no one trailing who can catch up. That also makes
it a good answer to man coverage, since a crossing route is the hardest route for a man defender
to stay on top of. The price is time: an 18-yard crosser needs three seconds or more, so Y-cross
asks a lot of the pass protection.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper: the Air Raid's small menu"}
The Air Raid was built at small colleges, not in the NFL. Hal Mumme, a high school and small
college coach, and Mike Leach, a former law student who had never played college football,
put it together at Iowa Wesleyan around 1989, took it to Valdosta State and then, in 1997, to the
University of Kentucky, where quarterback Tim Couch became the first pick of the 1999 NFL draft.
Leach went on to run it as a head coach at Texas Tech, Washington State and Mississippi State.[^airraid]

Their starting point was the passing game of LaVell Edwards's BYU teams, which they studied in
person, and their central idea was subtraction: run a handful of concepts (mesh, shallow cross,
Y-cross, four verticals, a few quick-game calls) from a handful of formations, and practice them
so many times that the quarterback and receivers react instead of think. Where an NFL playbook
might carry hundreds of pass plays, the Air Raid lived on a dozen. Its lesson for this chapter is
that a concept's power comes as much from repetition as from design: a quarterback who has read
the same curl-flat defender on the same Y-cross ten thousand times throws the ball before the
defender has finished deciding. The full story of the Air Raid's spread through college and then
the NFL is told in [The College Laboratory](../11-history/11-03-the-college-laboratory.qmd).
:::

## Man-beaters: mesh, the rub and the angle route

Everything so far is built to beat zone defenders, who guard areas and can be put between two
receivers. Man coverage changes the problem. Each defender has one receiver and follows him, so
there is no area to overload and no defender in two minds; the defense is betting its players can
stay with yours. The most common version in the NFL is
[Cover 1](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-1): a man on every receiver, one safety deep in the
middle, and often one more defender free to rush or to sit in the middle as a helper
([Man Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-02-man-coverage.qmd) builds it from the defense's side). The answer is to make *staying with* a receiver hard: send receivers across the
field, where their defenders have to chase them through traffic; break away from a defender's
leverage; or find a defender who is badly matched against the man he has to cover.

### Mesh

[**Mesh**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mesh) is the purest man-beater in football. Two
receivers from opposite sides run shallow crossing routes, five or six yards deep, that pass
within a yard or two of each other over the middle of the field. One runs his cross a step
higher than the other, and Air Raid coaches tell them to pass close enough to slap hands.

```{python}
#| label: fig-mesh
#| fig-cap: "Mesh against Cover 1 (man coverage with one deep safety), the version run by the Air Raid. H and Y cross at five to six yards over the ball, H a step above Y, so the defenders chasing them, the nickel ($) and the strong safety (SS), both ringed, have to get around one receiver to stay with the other. X and Z run corner routes and the back runs to the right flat. The progression in the traditional Air Raid order: (1) the corner route to the back's side, over the back's flat route; (2) the crossers, whichever comes out of the traffic first; (3) the back. Against man coverage, many teams look to the crossers first. Dotted lines are man assignments; the Mike rushes."
p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.5), cover1(), los=LOS, to_go=4)
protect(p, rushers=("WDE", "WDT", "SDT", "SDE"))
p.rush("MIKE", pts=[(-3.0, 0.4)], speed=4.0)
p.dropback(2.5)
route_to(p, "H", (3.8, -9.0), (6.0, -6.0), (6.4, 9.5))
route_to(p, "Y", (2.6, 8.4), (4.8, 5.0), (5.2, -10.5))
p.route("X", r.corner(10.0))
p.route("Z", r.corner(10.0))
route_to(p, "RB", (-3.4, 5.0), (0.2, 9.5), (1.2, 12.0))
for d_, t_ in (("LCB", "X"), ("RCB", "Z"), ("NB", "H"), ("SS", "Y"), ("WILL", "RB")):
    p.man(d_, t_)
p.highlight("NB", "SS")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (21.6, 21.2)), (2, (8.0, 10.6)), (2, (6.6, -12.4)), (3, (3.2, 10.6))],
            keys=["route", "man", "num", "ring"])
opening(fld, p, (5.6, 0.0), (2.6, 4.2))
say(fld, p, 9.2, -0.2, "the mesh point:\nclose enough to\nslap hands", color=OD)
tag(fld, p, "Man-beater (and zone holes)")
plt.show()
```

Against man coverage the two crossing paths do the work. The nickel chasing H has to get past Y
coming the other way, and the safety chasing Y has to get past H. One of them almost always loses
a step, and a receiver crossing the field with a one-step lead is nearly impossible to catch from
behind. Against zone the same routes simply settle: each crosser finds the space between two
underneath defenders and sits down facing the quarterback, so the concept is useful even when the
defense guesses right. The corner routes give the quarterback a high-low against the cornerbacks,
and keep the safety from crowding the middle.

Mesh came into the Air Raid from BYU and became its signature play; versions of it now appear in
every NFL playbook, often as a third-down call, when defenses play the most man coverage.

### The rub, and where it becomes a pick

Mesh works because of a specific kind of route. A
[**rub route**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rub-route) (also called a
[**pick route**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pick-route)) is a route designed to cross close
to a teammate's route, so a defender chasing one receiver has to go around the other. Crossers,
stacked receivers who release in opposite directions, and a slot receiver running a quick out
under an outside receiver's slant are all rubs. They are among the most effective plays in football
against man coverage, especially near the goal line, where the field is short and defenders play
tight.

They are also the most argued-about. The rules allow a receiver to run his route even if a defender
runs into him. They don't allow him to *block* a defender downfield before the ball is thrown and
touched. In the NFL, a receiver who deliberately makes contact with a defender more than one yard
past the line of scrimmage to get a teammate open, before the pass is touched, has committed
[offensive pass interference](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-offensive-pass-interference), a
10-yard penalty; contact within a yard of the line is allowed.[^opi] That is the line between a
rub and an illegal pick.

```{python}
#| label: fig-rub
#| fig-cap: "The same two routes, legal and illegal. Left: a legal rub. H runs his crossing route without breaking stride; the defender chasing Y has to go around him (dotted orange), loses a step, and Y comes free. No one blocked anybody. Right: an illegal pick. H stops his route four yards downfield, turns, and steps into Y's defender before the ball is thrown: that is offensive pass interference. The green band is the first yard past the line of scrimmage, where contact between receivers and defenders is allowed in the NFL."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 3.5))
for ax, legal in zip(axes, (True, False)):
    off = [O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, -3.0), O("Y", "WR", OFF_BALL, 3.0), O("C", "C", LINE_D, 0.0)]
    dfn = [D("NB", "NB", 1.6, 2.4, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 1.6, -2.4, "SS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=None)
    if legal:
        route_to(p, "H", (3.0, -3.0), (5.5, 0.0), (6.0, 6.5))
    else:
        route_to(p, "H", (3.0, -3.0), (4.0, -0.8))
    route_to(p, "Y", (2.5, 3.0), (4.6, 0.6), (5.2, -6.5))
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-9.5, 9.5), window=(-3.5, 10.5), show_ruler=False, width_in=3.2)
    x0, y0 = _P(fld, p, 0.0, -9.5)
    x1, y1 = _P(fld, p, 1.0, 9.5)
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((min(x0, x1), min(y0, y1)), abs(x1 - x0), abs(y1 - y0), fc=style.THIRD, alpha=0.18,
                           ec="none", zorder=1.5))
    if legal:
        branch(fld, p, [(1.6, 2.4), (3.2, 1.6), (4.4, 1.6), (3.6, -0.6), (4.4, -3.4), (4.8, -6.0)],
               color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4, dash=(0, (1, 1.6)))
        say(fld, p, 8.6, -4.0, "H runs his route;\nthe $ has to go\naround him", color=DD, fontsize=6.6)
        panel_title(ax, "Legal rub", fs=8.5)
    else:
        branch(fld, p, [(1.6, 2.4), (3.4, 1.4), (4.0, 0.2)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4)
        x, y = _P(fld, p, 4.1, -0.1)
        ax.plot([float(x)], [float(y)], marker="*", ms=13, color=DD, mec="white", mew=0.6, zorder=12)
        say(fld, p, 8.6, -3.6, "H stops and steps\ninto the $ 4 yards\ndownfield: flag", color=DD, fontsize=6.6)
        panel_title(ax, "Illegal pick (OPI)", fs=8.5)
    say(fld, p, -1.6, 6.6, "first yard:\ncontact allowed", color=READ_GREEN, fontsize=6.2)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.0)
plt.show()
```

The trouble is that the difference is often a matter of intent and inches, and officials have to
judge it at full speed. Offenses teach receivers to run through the defender's path rather than at
him, and to keep running; defenses teach their players to communicate ("switch" or "banjo,"
trading receivers instead of chasing through the traffic, which [Man Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-02-man-coverage.qmd)
explains) or to play zone, against which rubs gain nothing. How the officials enforce pass
interference, and how often they call it, is in
[Contact Rules and Penalties](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-03-contact-rules-and-penalties.qmd).

Here is mesh against man coverage, moving. Watch the strong safety chasing Y.

```{python}
#| label: fig-mesh-movie
#| fig-cap: "Mesh against Cover 1, simulated (BDB-format tracking, generated by gridiron rather than recorded). H and Y cross at about five yards over the ball. The nickel ($) trails H on his hip; the strong safety (SS, ringed), chasing Y, has to go around H, and by the time he is through, Y has a two-yard lead running away from him. The ball is out at about 1.9 seconds to Y, crossing toward the open left side of the field, before the deep safety can come down. Faint lines are where each player has been; the brown dashes are the ball in flight."
def mesh_play():
    p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.5), cover1(), los=LOS, to_go=4)
    protect(p)
    p.rush("MIKE", pts=[(-3.0, 0.4)], speed=4.0)
    p.dropback(2.5)
    route_to(p, "H", (3.8, -9.0), (6.0, -6.0), (6.4, 9.5), (6.6, 14.0))
    route_to(p, "Y", (2.6, 8.4), (4.8, 5.0), (5.2, -10.5), (5.4, -16.0))
    p.route("X", r.corner(10.0))
    p.route("Z", r.corner(10.0))
    route_to(p, "RB", (-3.4, 5.0), (0.2, 9.5), (1.2, 12.0))
    p.drop("FS", (15.0, 0.0), speed=2.0)
    p.pass_to("Y", t=1.9)
    set_track(p, "NB", chase(p, "NB", "H", lag=0.3, off=(-0.9, -0.6)))
    set_track(p, "SS", chase(p, "SS", "Y", lag=0.35, off=(-0.8, 0.8), detour=(0.75, 1.45, (3.2, 1.8)),
                             lag_after=0.75))
    set_track(p, "LCB", chase(p, "LCB", "X", lag=0.3, off=(-1.0, 0.8)))
    set_track(p, "RCB", chase(p, "RCB", "Z", lag=0.3, off=(-1.0, -0.8)))
    set_track(p, "WILL", chase(p, "WILL", "RB", lag=0.3, off=(1.6, -0.8), t_start=0.3, t_on=1.3))
    return p


mp = mesh_play()
mt = catch_time(mp)
notes = ["Man coverage: the $ on H, the SS\non Y, one safety deep, Mike rushes.",
```
