```{python}
         "H and Y cross at the mesh point.\nThe SS has to go around H.",
         "Ball out at 1.9 s: Y is a step and\na half clear, running away.",
         "Caught in stride, with open grass\nto the left and no one in front."]
play_movie(mp, [0.0, 1.0, 1.9, mt], notes=notes, lateral=(-22.0, 17.5), window=(-8.0, 13.0),
           rings=(("SS", style.THIRD),), throw_t=1.9)
```

### The angle route: a running back against a linebacker

The other classic man-beater uses a mismatch instead of traffic. In man coverage, somebody has to
cover the running back, and it is usually a linebacker: a player chosen for stopping runs, often
thirty pounds heavier than the back and a step slower in space. The
[**angle route**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-angle-route) (many playbooks call it the
[**Texas route**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-texas-route)) is built for that matchup. The
back releases toward the flat as if running a swing, and when the linebacker widens to chase him,
he plants and snaps back inside, angling upfield under the middle of the field.

```{python}
#| label: fig-angle
#| fig-cap: "The angle route against Cover 1, on the offense's right. The back (R) releases outside toward the flat, then plants and breaks back inside and upfield. The ringed Mike linebacker, covering him man-to-man, widens with the first step (dashed orange) and is left on the wrong side when the back cuts back. Y's seam and Z's go (blue) carry their defenders, the strong safety and the cornerback, deep and out of the area the angle route breaks into. The progression: (1) the angle route; (2) Y's seam, if the deep safety jumps the angle. The left side (grey) runs a slant and a go."
p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.5), cover1(extra={"MIKE": (4.5, 2.2), "WILL": (4.5, -2.6)}), los=LOS, to_go=6)
protect(p)
p.rush("WILL", pts=[(-3.0, -0.6)], speed=4.0)
p.dropback(2.5)
route_to(p, "RB", (-4.0, 4.8), (-1.6, 7.0), (5.4, 2.6))
p.route("Y", r.seam(20.0))
p.route("Z", r.go(21.0))
for d_, t_ in (("LCB", "X"), ("RCB", "Z"), ("NB", "H"), ("SS", "Y"), ("MIKE", "RB")):
    p.man(d_, t_)
p.highlight("MIKE")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (6.8, 0.6)), (2, (19.8, 10.6))],
            ghosts=[[(-0.7, -15.0), (2.3, -15.0), (6.5, -10.2)], [(-1.5, -9.0), (19.0, -9.0)]],
            keys=["route", "ghost", "man", "react", "num", "ring"])
branch(fld, p, [(4.5, 2.2), (3.4, 5.0), (3.0, 7.6)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4)
say(fld, p, -4.8, 9.4, "release\noutside...", color=OD)
say(fld, p, 9.4, 4.4, "...snap back\ninside", color=OD)
tag(fld, p, "Man-beater: the linebacker")
plt.show()
```

The angle route is a cousin of the option route of [Passing Fundamentals](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd):
the back is breaking away from his defender's leverage. Against zone it still works if the routes
outside clear the area, because the back settles in the hook zone the linebacker has left, though
the throw is worth less. It is also why offenses love backs who can run routes: a back who wins
on the angle route forces the defense either to cover him with a safety, which takes a defender
out of the run fit, or to accept the mismatch.

## Deep shots: four verticals, post-wheel, scissors and yankee

The last four concepts go deep. They exist because a defense that never has to worry about the
deep ball will crowd every short and intermediate route in this chapter; somebody has to make the
deepest defenders defend something. Each of them stretches the *deep* defenders, the safeties
and the cornerbacks who play over the top, rather than the linebackers.

### Four verticals

[**Four verticals**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-four-verticals) is the simplest idea in the
passing game: four receivers run straight up the field at once. The two outside receivers stay
near the sideline, the two inside receivers run up the seams, a few yards outside the hashes. The
defense has only two or three deep defenders, so somebody is one-on-one, or nobody is there at all.

```{python}
#| label: fig-four-verts
#| fig-cap: "Four verticals against Cover 3. X and Z run go routes outside the numbers; H and Y run up the seams just outside the hashes. Three deep defenders face four vertical routes: the cornerbacks have the outside receivers in their deep thirds, so the ringed free safety, alone in the middle third, has two seams to cover. The progression: (1) the seam he doesn't take, read from his first steps; (2) the back, who checks for a blitzer and then settles over the ball, if the curl-flat defenders sink with the seams. The outside go routes are the first look only against a cornerback who sits short, as in Cover 2."
p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.5), cover3(nb_side=1), los=LOS, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(3.0)
for k in ("X", "Z"):
    p.route(k, r.path((10.0, 0.4), (24.0, 1.0)))
for k in ("H", "Y"):
    p.route(k, r.path((7.0, -1.4), (24.0, -3.0)))
route_to(p, "RB", (-3.6, 2.8), (4.0, 1.0), delay=0.8)
p.drop("FS", (17.0, 0.0))
p.drop("LCB", (17.0, -16.8))
p.drop("RCB", (17.0, 16.8))
p.drop("NB", (11.0, 9.0))
p.drop("SS", (11.0, -9.0))
p.drop("MIKE", (8.5, 3.0))
p.drop("WILL", (8.5, -4.0))
p.highlight("FS")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (22.4, -8.4)), (1, (22.4, 8.4)), (2, (5.8, 0.0))],
            stretch="Horizontal stretch: the deep defenders")
bracket(fld, p, 20.0, -6.0, 6.0, "", color=DD)
say(fld, p, 18.2, 0.0, "one safety,\ntwo seams", color=DD)
plt.show()
```

The arithmetic is the point. Against [Cover 3](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-3), three deep
defenders divide the field into thirds; four vertical routes put two receivers in the middle third,
where there is only one defender. If he leans toward one seam, the quarterback throws the other.
Against Cover 2, with two deep safeties each guarding a half, the seams split the safeties and the
outside receivers attack the gap between the squatting cornerbacks and the safeties along the
sideline, the same hole smash attacks. The concept forces the deep defenders to show where they are,
and the quarterback reads them, not the underneath ones. The defense's best answer is to
have the curl-flat defenders run with the seams for the first several yards, so the safety only
has to help on one of them; how Cover 3 defenses do that is a large part of
[The Cover 3 Family](../06-pass-coverage/06-03-cover-3-family.qmd).

```{python}
#| label: fig-four-verts-movie
#| fig-cap: "Four verticals against Cover 3, simulated (BDB-format tracking, generated by gridiron). The cornerbacks bail with the outside receivers, the curl-flat defenders run with the seams for a few steps and then let them go, and the free safety (ringed) has to choose. The quarterback looks to his right as he drops, and the safety drifts that way, toward Y; the ball goes to H on the left seam, behind the curl-flat defender and in front of the cornerback, about 25 yards downfield."
def verts_play():
    p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.5), cover3(nb_side=1), los=LOS, to_go=10)
    protect(p)
    p.dropback(3.0)
    for k in ("X", "Z"):
        p.route(k, r.path((10.0, 0.4), (30.0, 1.2)))
    for k in ("H", "Y"):
        p.route(k, r.path((7.0, -1.4), (30.0, -3.2)))
    route_to(p, "RB", (-3.6, 2.8), (4.0, 1.0), delay=0.8)
    p.drop("LCB", (27.5, -17.0), speed=7.0)
    p.drop("RCB", (27.5, 17.0), speed=7.0)
    p.path("FS", [(1.5, 0.0), (3.0, 2.6), (5.5, 4.8)], speed=4.2, delay=0.2)
    p.drop("NB", (9.0, 8.0), speed=4.0)
    p.drop("SS", (9.5, -8.5), speed=4.0)
    p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, 3.0))
    p.drop("WILL", (8.0, -4.0))
    p.pass_to("H", t=2.2)
    return p


vp = verts_play()
with ball_speed(24.0):
    vt = catch_time(vp)
notes = ["Three deep defenders (two CBs, FS)\nagainst four vertical routes.",
         "The CBs bail with X and Z; the seams\nrun past the curl-flat defenders.",
         "The QB looks right; the FS leans to\nY. Ball out at 2.2 s to H's seam.",
         "Caught about 25 yards deep, in the\nmiddle third the FS left."]
with ball_speed(24.0):
    play_movie(vp, [0.0, 1.2, 2.2, vt], notes=notes, lateral=(-24.0, 24.0), window=(-8.0, 30.5),
               rings=(("FS", style.THIRD),), throw_t=2.2)
```

Notice what the quarterback did with his eyes. He looked toward Y as he dropped, and the safety,
who reads the quarterback, drifted that way. Moving a defender with your eyes is called a
[look-off](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-look-off), and it's an essential skill for any concept
that reads a single deep defender ([Quarterback Play](04-07-quarterback-play.qmd) has more).

Four verticals goes back at least to the 1970s and 1980s, when BYU, Don Coryell's San Diego
Chargers and the [run-and-shoot](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-run-and-shoot) offenses of
Mouse Davis all built passing games around vertical routes; the Air Raid made it one of its core
calls.<!-- VERIFY: the four-verticals lineage (BYU under Edwards, Coryell's Chargers, run-and-shoot under Mouse Davis) as commonly described; Brown, The Essential Smart Football. --> In the modern NFL it rarely looks
like four straight lines. Andy Reid's Chiefs, for one, have run many variations, with Travis Kelce on
a seam route that bends inside or holds straight depending on the safeties (a route conversion, as
below) and speed outside to stretch the cornerbacks.<!-- VERIFY: Chiefs' four-verticals variants with a Kelce seam-read/bender; general description, no specific play claimed. -->

### Post-wheel

[**Post-wheel**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-post-wheel) stretches the deep defender on one
side, inside and out. The outside receiver runs a post, angling toward the middle at about 12
yards; the inside receiver (or a back) runs a wheel, out toward the flat and then straight up the
sideline, into the space the post receiver just left.

```{python}
#| label: fig-post-wheel
#| fig-cap: "Post-wheel to the offense's right against Cover 3. Z runs a post; Y, from the slot, runs a wheel, out toward the flat and then up the sideline. The ringed cornerback, whose deep third covers both routes, has to choose: stay outside on the wheel and the post breaks open inside him, in front of the free safety; carry the post inside and the wheel goes up the sideline behind the curl-flat defender ($), who can't run with it. The progression: (1) the wheel; (2) the post; (3) the back, checking down on the left. Against man coverage, the wheel also pits a slot receiver or back against a linebacker or nickel running backward."
p = Play(spread(), cover3(nb_side=1), los=LOS, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(3.0)
route_to(p, "Z", (10.0, 15.0), (19.5, 7.5))
route_to(p, "Y", (-0.8, 11.5), (1.5, 14.5), (5.5, 18.5), (21.0, 19.4))
rb_n = swing(p, -1)
p.drop("RCB", (13.5, 15.0))
p.drop("NB", (4.5, 13.0))
p.drop("FS", (16.0, 0.0))
p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, 3.0))
p.drop("WILL", (8.0, -4.0))
p.drop("SS", (7.0, -12.0))
p.drop("LCB", (17.0, -16.6))
p.highlight("RCB")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (21.0, 21.9)), (2, (21.2, 7.0)), (3, rb_n)],
            ghosts=[[(-0.7, -15.0), (11.3, -15.0), (11.3, -5.0)], [(-1.5, -9.0), (5.0, -9.0), (5.2, -7.0)]],
            stretch="Horizontal stretch: the cornerback")
say(fld, p, 10.0, 22.4, "wheel", color=OD)
say(fld, p, 12.6, 9.2, "post", color=OD)
plt.show()
```

Post-wheel is a [conflict](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-conflict-defender) for a defender who is
trained to stay deep and outside. A Cover 3 cornerback is taught to keep everything in front of him
and to the inside, and to hand the post over to the free safety; the wheel is the route he is least
ready for, because it starts as a harmless flat route and becomes a deep route in front of him only
after he has started to turn inside. Against man coverage it is better still: the wheel puts a
slot receiver or a running back against a nickel or a linebacker who has to turn and run up the
sideline with him.

### Scissors

[**Scissors**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-scissors) is post-wheel's mirror image, aimed at
two-high coverages. The outside receiver runs a post and the inside receiver a corner route, so
their paths cross at 10 to 12 yards like the blades of a pair of scissors.

```{python}
#| label: fig-scissors
#| fig-cap: "Scissors to the offense's right against Quarters. Z runs a post, Y a corner route; their paths cross at about 12 yards. The ringed strong safety reads Y, as Quarters asks him to: if he widens with Y's corner route, the post breaks open inside, between the two safeties; if he stays inside on the post, the corner route is one-on-one against a nickel who can't run with it. The cornerback, playing Z from outside leverage, can't take the post away by himself. The progression: (1) the post; (2) the corner; (3) the back, checking down on the left."
p = Play(spread(), quarters(), los=LOS, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(3.0)
route_to(p, "Z", (9.3, 15.0), (19.5, 5.0))
route_to(p, "Y", (8.5, 9.0), (18.5, 18.6))
rb_n = swing(p, -1)
p.drop("SS", (15.0, 11.0))
p.drop("RCB", (14.0, 16.4))
p.drop("NB", (8.5, 10.0))
p.drop("FS", (15.0, -8.0))
p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, 3.0))
p.drop("WILL", (8.0, -5.0))
p.drop("LCB", (15.0, -16.0))
p.highlight("SS")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (21.2, 3.4)), (2, (20.0, 20.6)), (3, rb_n)],
            ghosts=[[(-0.7, -15.0), (11.3, -15.0), (11.3, -5.0)], [(-1.5, -9.0), (5.0, -9.0), (5.2, -7.0)]],
            stretch="Horizontal stretch: the safety")
point_to(fld, p, (17.0, 0.0), (12.0, 12.4), "the blades cross\nat about 12 yards", color=OD)
plt.show()
```

The defender in conflict is the safety on that side. In Quarters, as in dagger, he reads the inside
receiver: if that receiver goes vertical, the safety goes with him. Scissors uses that rule twice.
The inside receiver goes vertical, so the safety starts to carry him, and then breaks outside on the
corner route, pulling the safety toward the sideline; the outside receiver, meanwhile, breaks
inside on the post, behind the space the safety just left and inside the cornerback, who is playing
him from the outside. Against man coverage the crossing paths add a rub at depth.

### Yankee

[**Yankee**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-yankee) is a two-man deep shot. One receiver runs a
post from one side; the other runs a deep over route, a crosser at about 18 to 22 yards, from the
other side. Both routes finish in the deep middle, one above the single deep safety and one in
front of him. It is almost always run off
[play-action](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-play-action), with a fake handoff to freeze the
linebackers, and with [max protection](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-max-protect), seven or eight
blockers, because both routes take three seconds or more to develop.

```{python}
#| label: fig-yankee
#| fig-cap: "Yankee against Cover 3, from an under-center formation with two tight ends (12 personnel). The quarterback fakes a handoff to the back (R), then sets up deep. X runs a post from the left; Z runs a deep over from the right, climbing to about 20 yards. The ringed free safety, alone in the deep middle, faces a high-low: (1) the post if he comes up on the over; (2) the over if he stays deep with the post. The five linemen, Y and the back block (seven-man protection); U helps for a moment, then releases late to the flat as the outlet (3). The linebackers step up toward the run fake (short orange arrows), which empties the area the over route crosses."
off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", UNDER, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"),
                 O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.8), O("U", "TE", LINE_D, -4.8, "U"),
                 O("X", "WR", OFF_BALL, -15.0), O("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 15.0)]
dfn = dline() + [D("SAM", "SAM", 4.0, 5.8, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 0.6, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -3.4, "W"),
                 D("SS", "SS", 8.0, -7.0, "SS"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -16.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 16.0, "CB"),
                 D("FS", "FS", 13.5, 0.0, "FS")]
dfn = [q.moved(w=-6.6) if q.key == "WDE" else q.moved(w=6.6) if q.key == "SDE" else q for q in dfn]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.block("Y", pts=[(-1.0, 0.0)])
p.path("QB", [(-2.6, 1.2)], speed=4.5)
p.path("QB", [(-6.2, 0.0)], speed=4.0)
p.run("RB", [(1.0, 1.2), (2.0, 1.6)], speed=5.0)
route_to(p, "X", (10.5, -15.0), (22.5, -2.0))
route_to(p, "Z", (6.0, 13.5), (15.5, 2.0), (19.5, -13.0))
route_to(p, "U", (-0.4, -6.0), (1.4, -10.0), delay=1.4)
for k, to in (("SAM", (3.0, 4.6)), ("MIKE", (3.4, 1.2)), ("WILL", (3.4, -2.4))):
    p.path(k, [(to[0] - p.players[k].d, to[1] - p.players[k].w)], speed=3.0)
p.drop("FS", (16.5, 0.0))
p.drop("LCB", (17.0, -16.6))
p.drop("RCB", (17.0, 16.6))
p.drop("SS", (8.0, -11.0))
p.highlight("FS")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (24.0, -0.4)), (2, (21.4, -14.6)), (3, (3.0, -11.8))],
            keys=["route", "run", "drop", "num", "ring"],
            stretch="Vertical stretch: the deep safety")
say(fld, p, 24.4, -9.5, "post over the top", color=OD)
say(fld, p, 13.6, 9.6, "deep over\nunder the FS", color=OD)
say(fld, p, -6.6, 5.0, "run fake", color=OD)
plt.show()
```

Why does it work? The run fake does half the job. Linebackers are taught to stop the run first,
so they step forward when they see a handoff, and that step takes them out of the path of the deep
over, which crosses behind them at a depth no underneath defender can reach. The other half is a
high-low on the one man left: the free safety in the middle of the field can sink to take away the
post or come forward to take away the over, not both. Sean McVay's Rams made yankee one of the
signature shot plays of the late 2010s, and it now appears in most NFL playbooks that come from
the Shanahan and McVay family of offenses.<!-- VERIFY: yankee as a signature Rams/McVay play-action shot (e.g., 2018 Rams); Shanahan-tree usage. --> The price is the
protection: with seven or eight blockers, only two or three receivers go out, so if the safety
plays it perfectly the quarterback has very little to throw to. How play-action works,
and why the fake works even when the run game doesn't, belongs to
[Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens](04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd).

## Tags and route conversions

Fourteen concepts sounds like a lot, but a real playbook has many more, and most of the extras
aren't new concepts at all. They are the same concepts with a word added. A
[tag](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tag) is a word added to a play call that changes one
player's assignment and leaves everyone else's alone. "Mesh" tells all five receivers what to do;
"Mesh, Z-wheel" keeps mesh intact except for Z, who runs a wheel instead of his corner route. Tags
let a play-caller adjust a concept to a defense's habits (a cornerback who jumps corner routes, a
safety who cheats toward the crossers) without teaching a new play.

The second tool is subtler, and it explains how one call can be right against several coverages.
A [**route conversion**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-route-conversion) is a rule built into a
route that changes it according to the coverage the receiver sees. The receiver doesn't wait for
the quarterback to tell him; he reads the defense himself, usually the safeties, and the
quarterback, reading the same thing, knows where he will be.

```{python}
#| label: fig-conversion
#| fig-cap: "One route conversion: the seam route in four verticals. The receiver (Y) reads the safeties as he runs. Left, middle of the field closed (one deep safety): he stays on his landmark just outside the hash and bends slightly away from the safety, keeping him in conflict with the other seam. Right, middle of the field open (two deep safeties): the middle is empty, so at about 12 yards he bends inside, splitting the safeties, into the space between them (green). Same call, same receiver; the coverage picks the route."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 3.7))
for ax, one_high in zip(axes, (True, False)):
    off = [O("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, 8.0), O("C", "C", LINE_D, 0.0)]
    if one_high:
        dfn = [D("FS", "FS", 13.5, 0.0, "FS")]
    else:
        dfn = [D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -8.5, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 12.5, 8.5, "SS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=None)
    if one_high:
        route_to(p, "Y", (8.0, 7.6), (22.0, 6.6))
        p.drop("FS", (17.0, 0.0))
    else:
        route_to(p, "Y", (11.0, 7.6), (21.0, 1.2))
        p.drop("FS", (16.0, -10.0))
        p.drop("SS", (16.0, 10.0))
    p.highlight(*[q.key for q in dfn])
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-13.5, 15.5), window=(-3.5, 24.5), show_ruler=False, width_in=3.2)
    if one_high:
        say(fld, p, 22.6, -6.0, "one safety:\nstay on the\nlandmark", color=OD, fontsize=6.8)
        panel_title(ax, "MOFC: stay vertical", fs=8.5)
    else:
        opening(fld, p, (20.0, 1.0), (4.0, 7.0))
        say(fld, p, 9.0, -6.0, "two safeties:\nbend into the\nempty middle", color=OD, fontsize=6.8)
        panel_title(ax, "MOFO: bend inside", fs=8.5)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.0)
plt.show()
```

You've already met the most important conversion. The
[option route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-option-route) of
[Passing Fundamentals](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd), which some systems call the *choice route*,
is a conversion with two branches: against man, break away from the defender's leverage; against
zone, sit in the hole. Others are everywhere in this chapter. The smash corner route flattens under
a two-high safety and pushes deeper against one-high. The levels and mesh crossers keep running
against man and settle against zone. The dagger dig sits down in a window against zone and keeps
crossing against man.

The Patriots of the Tom Brady era were the model of an offense built on conversions. Their
Erhardt-Perkins system (named for Ron Erhardt and Ray Perkins, who coached together on New England's
staff in the 1970s, and carried forward by Bill Parcells to Bill Belichick and Josh McDaniels) named
whole concepts with short words, so a quarterback could call them at the line, and gave its slot
receivers wide freedom to read and adjust their routes after the snap.[^ep] That's why New England's
passing game seemed to have an answer for every defense without a thousand plays: the same few
concepts, each with branches. The system's history and its rivals are in
[Offensive Systems and Languages](04-08-offensive-systems-and-languages.qmd).

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In a video game, the receiver runs the route drawn on the play art, whatever the defense does, and
you press a button for the one you want. In the NFL, a large share of routes are conditional: the
receiver converts the route against the coverage, the quarterback has to read the same thing and
throw to where the receiver *will* be, and a mismatch between their reads is one of the commonest
causes of an interception that looks, on the broadcast, like the quarterback threw to nobody. When
an announcer says a receiver and quarterback "weren't on the same page," that's usually what
happened: one of them saw man and the other saw zone.
:::

## The quarterback's side: one clock for every concept

Each plate in this chapter carried a progression, and they all follow the same pattern. That
pattern is the real skill of dropback passing, so it is worth spelling out.

**Before the snap**, the quarterback identifies the shell (one high safety or two), checks the
leverage of the defenders over the receivers in the concept, and asks the question every concept
poses: *who is the defender in conflict, and where is he?* If the concept is called to both sides,
as smash often is, this is when he picks the side. If the defense shows a blitz, he checks the
protection and his hot route ([Pass Protection](04-02-pass-protection.qmd)).

**At the snap**, his eyes go to the conflict defender, not to a receiver. His drop is timed so
that the first read is ready as his back foot lands: on smash, the corner route breaks as he hits
the bottom of his drop; on dagger, the dig arrives a beat later, which is why dagger takes a deeper
drop or a hitch step.

**After the first look**, he moves to the next read with his feet as well as his eyes. Each
*hitch*, a short step up into the pocket, resets his feet for the next throw. A typical dropback
progression gets two or three looks before the rush arrives; the last is the
[checkdown](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-checkdown), the short throw to a back that keeps the
play from losing yards. As [Passing Fundamentals](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd) showed with FTN's
charting, more than half of all throws go to the first read, and those are the quickest and most
valuable: the concept is at its best when its first answer is right.

**High to low or low to high?** Most vertical stretches are read from the top down: look at the
deep route first, because if it's open it's the bigger gain, then come down to the short one, which
will still be there. Some are read the other way: the drive shallow and the mesh crossers are
looked at first against man, because a crosser who wins does so immediately. Coaches choose the
order to fit the concept's timing and the down and distance. On third-and-8, a progression starts
with the route that reaches the line to gain.

The table gathers the fourteen concepts, the family each belongs to, the defender it puts in a bind
and the coverage it's built to beat. The last column is the subject of
[What Beats What](../08-the-chess-match/08-01-concepts-versus-coverages.qmd), which pairs concepts
with coverages in detail; how each coverage defends these concepts is in Part 6, beginning with
[Coverage Fundamentals](../06-pass-coverage/06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd) and, for four verticals,
[The Cover 3 Family](../06-pass-coverage/06-03-cover-3-family.qmd).

| Concept | Family | Defender in conflict | Built to beat | Typical progression |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Smash | Vertical stretch | Cornerback | Cover 2 | corner → hitch → back |
| Flood (sail) | Vertical, three levels | Curl-flat defender | Cover 3 | sail → flat (go if the corner sits) |
| Curl-flat | Triangle | Curl-flat and hook defenders | Cover 3, zone | curl → flat → hook |
| Levels | Vertical stretch | Hook linebacker | Zone | dig → in → back |
| Drive | Vertical; also a man-beater | Middle linebacker | Zone and man | shallow → dig → back |
| Shallow cross | Vertical; also a man-beater | Middle linebacker | Zone and man | shallow → dig or sit → back |
| Dagger | Vertical stretch | Safety and hook defenders | Two-high (Quarters, Cover 2) | seam → dig → back |
| Y-cross | Vertical, three levels | Far curl-flat defender | Cover 3, man | cross → flat → back |
| Mesh | Man-beater | Man defenders on the crossers | Man (Cover 1, Cover 0) | corner → crossers → back |
| Angle (Texas) | Man-beater | Linebacker covering the back | Man | angle → seam |
| Four verticals | Horizontal, deep | Free safety | Cover 3, Cover 2 | seam away from the safety → back |
| Post-wheel | Horizontal, deep | Cornerback | Cover 3, man | wheel → post → back |
| Scissors | Horizontal, deep | Safety | Quarters | post → corner → back |
| Yankee | Vertical, deep | Free safety | One-high | post → over → outlet |

: The fourteen dropback concepts at a glance. "Built to beat" is the concept's best matchup, not its only one. {#tbl-concepts}

## Film room

The concepts above are in every NFL playbook. A few teams built an identity on them, and watching
those teams is the fastest way to learn to see the concepts at game speed.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Texas Tech 2007–2008"}
**Mesh and Y-cross, rep after rep.** Mike Leach's Texas Tech teams were the Air Raid at full
volume. In 2007, quarterback Graham Harrell threw for 5,705 yards and freshman receiver Michael
Crabtree caught 134 passes for 1,962 yards and 22 touchdowns; Crabtree won the Biletnikoff Award as
the nation's best receiver that season and again in 2008.[^ttu] Nearly all of it came out of the
same small menu of concepts drawn in this chapter: mesh, shallow cross, Y-cross and four verticals,
from wide 2x2 and trips formations with enormous splits between the offensive linemen.

**What to notice on the tape:** the mesh point, two crossers passing over the center close enough to
touch, and a defender losing a step as he goes around; Harrell's eyes on the curl-flat defender on
Y-cross, and the ball arriving as the crosser came into the window; and how *few* different plays
there were. The defense knew what was coming, and it didn't matter, because the offense had run
each concept thousands of times against every look. Leach's former quarterback Kliff Kingsbury later
brought the same concepts to the NFL as the Arizona Cardinals' head coach (2019–2022).[^kingsbury]
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Los Angeles Rams 2018"}
**Yankee and the play-action shot.** In Sean McVay's second season, the Rams went 13–3 and reached
Super Bowl LIII, where they lost to New England 13–3. Jared Goff threw for 4,688 yards and 32
touchdowns.[^rams] Their passing game ran on a single foundation: line up in the same formation with
three receivers, run outside-zone handoffs out of it, and throw play-action shots from the same look,
yankee chief among them. On throws of 20 yards or more in the air, the Rams averaged about +0.77 EPA
per attempt, third-best in the league, against a league average of about +0.37.[^deep18]

**What to notice on the tape:** the linebackers' first step on the run fake, *toward* the line;
the deep over crossing behind them at 18 to 20 yards; and the free safety in the middle, who has to
decide between the over in front of him and the post behind him. Goff often had only two routes to
choose from, and his decision was made by one defender.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Kansas City Chiefs 2018"}
**Four verticals with a 50-touchdown quarterback.** In Patrick Mahomes's first season as the starter
he threw for 5,097 yards and 50 touchdowns and was named the league's MVP. Andy Reid's offense threw
deep more than almost anyone: 15% of the Chiefs' attempts traveled 20 yards or more in the air (fifth
in the league; the league average was 12%), and those throws were worth about +0.75 EPA each, fourth
best.[^kc18] Tyreek Hill's speed outside and Travis Kelce up the seam made four verticals and its
variants a constant threat.

**What to notice on the tape:** the deep defenders' first steps. With Hill on the outside, cornerbacks
bailed at the snap, which opened everything underneath; with Kelce on a seam, the middle safety had to
choose. Watch Kelce's seam bend or stay straight as he reads the safeties, the route conversion in
action, and Mahomes moving the safety with his eyes before throwing the other way.
:::

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it: name the concept"}
**Before the snap**

- **Find the shell.** One deep safety or two? Smash, dagger and scissors are two-high beaters;
  flood, four verticals, post-wheel and yankee feast on one-high.
- **Find the pairs.** Look at each side of the formation and ask which two or three receivers could
  work together. A slot and an outside receiver on the same side are a likely smash, flood or
  post-wheel; two slots on opposite sides are a likely mesh or shallow cross.
- **Man or zone?** Pressed corners, a defender following a motion man across the formation: think
  man, and think mesh, rubs and the angle route.

**On the replay** (the end-zone camera or the skycam is best)

- **Find the two-receiver combination on the side the ball went to.** Was one route above the other
  (a vertical stretch), side by side (horizontal), three in a triangle, or crossing (a man-beater)?
  Name the stretch, then name the concept.
- **Find the defender in conflict.** Who stood between the two routes? What did he do? The ball went
  to the receiver he didn't take.
- **Count the time.** A dropback concept takes about "one-thousand-one, one-thousand-two,
  one-thousand-three." If the ball is out before "two," it was the quick game.

**For your prediction log** ([How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd)):
on each third-and-medium, write the shell you see and the concept family you expect (two-high:
smash or dagger; man: mesh or rubs). Check yourself on the replay.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: two high, corners squatting"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-smash
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-8. The offense has called smash to both sides. The defense shows two deep safeties at about 13 yards, each well outside the hash, and both cornerbacks squatting five yards off with outside leverage. On the right, the nickel ($) is lined up inside Y; on the left, the Will linebacker (W) is walked out over H."
p = Play(spread(), cover2(extra={"WILL": (4.5, -7.4), "FS": (13.0, -9.0), "SS": (13.0, 9.0)}), los=55, to_go=8)
protect(p)
p.dropback(2.5)
for k in ("X", "Z"):
    p.route(k, r.hitch(5.0))
route_to(p, "Y", (8.5, 9.0), (16.0, 17.5))
route_to(p, "H", (8.5, -9.0), (16.0, -17.5))
p.highlight("LCB", "RCB", color=DD)
fld = draw(p, lateral="full", window=(-8.5, 22.5))
say(fld, p, 17.6, 0.0, "two deep, both\nwell outside the hash", color=DD)
plt.show()
```

**Which route is the quarterback's first look, which defender does he watch, and what would make him
come off it?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The corner route, read off the cornerback, with one eye on the safety.** This is the picture smash
was built for: Cover 2, two deep safeties and cornerbacks squatting short. Either side will do, because
the defense is the same on both; many quarterbacks pick the side of the field with more room or the
receiver they trust more.

After the snap, he watches the cornerback on that side. If the cornerback sits on the hitch (Cover 2
tells him to), the corner route is open behind him, and the throw has to get there before the safety,
who starts thirteen yards deep and well inside the corner route, can get over to the sideline. If the cornerback sinks under the corner route instead, the hitch is open in front of him.

What would make him come off it? Two things. If the safety on that side doesn't backpedal but runs
for the sideline at the snap, he is taking the corner route away, and the hitch (or the other side) is
the throw. And if the cornerback bails deep at the snap, the "Cover 2" was a disguise for Cover 3 (see
[Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)):
the corner route is now covered from above, and the hitch is the answer.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: press man on third down"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-man
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-4. Both cornerbacks are pressed on X and Z, the nickel ($) is pressed on H, the strong safety stands across from Y, the Will is over the back, and one safety is deep in the middle. Before the snap, H went in motion across the formation and back; the nickel followed him all the way and back again."
p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.5), cover1(), los=72, to_go=4)
fld = draw(p, lateral="full", window=(-8.5, 17.5))
for d_, t_ in (("LCB", "X"), ("RCB", "Z"), ("NB", "H"), ("SS", "Y"), ("WILL", "RB")):
    a_, b_ = p.players[d_], p.players[t_]
    branch(fld, p, [(a_.d, a_.w), (b_.d, b_.w)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=0.9, dash=(0, (1, 2)), end="none")
say(fld, p, 16.0, 0.0, "one deep safety", color=DD)
plt.show()
```

**The offense has three concepts on its call sheet for this situation: flood, four verticals and mesh.
Which one should it run, and why?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Mesh.** Everything here says man coverage: pressed cornerbacks, a defender over every receiver,
a single safety deep, and, the clincher, a nickel who followed H across the formation and back on the
motion. Zone defenders don't travel with a motion man; man defenders do
([Motion and Shifts](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd)).

Against man, the zone-beaters lose their point. Flood's three levels stretch a curl-flat defender who
doesn't exist; each receiver just has a defender following him. Four verticals is a better man answer
but needs three seconds and a receiver who can beat a pressed cornerback deep, which is a big ask on
third-and-4. Mesh is built for this: the two crossers run at five or six yards, close to the line to
gain, and the defenders pressing H and Y have to fight through each other's traffic. One of the
crossers usually comes free within two seconds, running away from his man.

What should worry the offense? The Mike linebacker. In Cover 1, the defender not assigned to anyone
often sits in the middle as a [robber](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-robber), exactly where the
crossers meet. The quarterback has to find him before the snap and throw the crosser running away
from him.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: one safety, two seams"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-verts
#| fig-cap: "Second-and-10 from the offense's own 30. Four verticals is called. The defense shows one deep safety, but he has lined up over the left hash rather than in the middle, at about 14 yards. The cornerbacks are seven yards off with outside leverage."
p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.5), cover3(nb_side=1, extra={"FS": (14.0, -4.0)}), los=40, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(3.0)
for k in ("X", "Z"):
    p.route(k, r.path((10.0, 0.4), (24.0, 1.0)))
for k in ("H", "Y"):
    p.route(k, r.path((7.0, -1.4), (24.0, -3.0)))
p.highlight("FS")
fld = draw(p, lateral="full", window=(-8.5, 26.5))
point_to(fld, p, (18.6, -12.5), (14.0, -4.0), "FS over the\nleft hash", color=DD)
plt.show()
```

**Which seam should the quarterback expect to throw, and what should he do with his eyes?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Y's seam, on the right, away from the safety, and he should look left first.** One safety means
Cover 3 (or Cover 1), and against four verticals that single safety is the man in conflict: two seams,
one defender. He has already shaded toward the left seam before the snap, so the right seam starts
with a head start of several yards.

But a good safety lines up off-center on purpose sometimes, to bait the throw and then race back to
the middle. The quarterback's answer is his eyes: look at H's seam on the left as he drops, holding
the safety there, then turn and throw to Y. That's the
[look-off](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-look-off) from the four-verticals animation. If the safety
ignores the eyes and runs right at the snap, H's seam on the left is open behind him, and if both
seams are covered by the curl-flat defenders carrying them, the back underneath, settling over the
ball, is the checkdown.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- A **pass concept** is a set of routes built to work together, usually by putting one or two
  defenders in a bind; it has a name so the whole offense can learn and call it as a unit, from any
  formation.
- Concepts come in **four families**: **vertical stretches** (high-low: smash, flood, levels, drive,
  shallow cross, dagger, Y-cross, yankee), **horizontal stretches** (side to side, deep: four verticals,
  post-wheel, scissors), **triangles** (three receivers around two defenders: curl-flat, snag) and
  **man-beaters** (crossers, rubs and mismatches: mesh, the angle route).
- Each concept is built to beat certain coverages: smash and dagger attack **two-high**, flood, four
  verticals, post-wheel and yankee attack **one-high**, and mesh and the angle route attack **man**.
  That is why the quarterback's pre-snap read starts with the safeties.
- The quarterback reads **the defender in conflict, not the receivers**, and his progression runs on
  his feet: the first read as his back foot lands, the next on a hitch, the checkdown last.
- **Rub routes** beat man coverage by making defenders run through traffic; a receiver who deliberately
  blocks a defender more than a yard downfield before the ball is touched commits **offensive pass
  interference**.
- **Tags** change one route in a concept; **route conversions** let a route change itself by coverage,
  so one call can be right against several defenses. The **intermediate middle** of the field is the
  most valuable place to throw, and most of these concepts exist to get the ball there.

- **From diagrams to real tracking data.** The two animations above are gridiron simulations in NFL Big
  Data Bowl coordinates. The 2025 Big Data Bowl release (2022 season, weeks 1–9) charts every receiver's
  route on every play, so you can find real four-verticals and mesh calls and watch them. The data needs a
  free Kaggle login, so this code is not run when the book is built.

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (real Big Data Bowl tracking; not run in the build)"
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
player_play = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/player_play.csv")
routes = player_play.dropna(subset=["routeRan"])

# four verticals: at least four receivers on GO routes on the same play
gos = routes[routes["routeRan"] == "GO"].groupby(["gameId", "playId"]).size()
verts = gos[gos >= 4].reset_index()[["gameId", "playId"]]

# mesh-like: two or more crossing routes on the same play, thrown to a crosser
cross = routes[routes["routeRan"] == "CROSS"].groupby(["gameId", "playId"]).size()
mesh = cross[cross >= 2].reset_index()[["gameId", "playId"]]
mesh = mesh.merge(plays[["gameId", "playId", "passResult", "pff_manZone"]], on=["gameId", "playId"])
mesh_vs_man = mesh[mesh["pff_manZone"] == "Man"]

g, pl = verts.iloc[0][["gameId", "playId"]]
trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl)
show_animation(one, times=[0.0, 1.2, 2.4, 3.2])   # snap, release, safety's choice, catch
```

Median time to throw: 2.2 seconds for throws behind the line of scrimmage, 2.3 seconds for 0–9 air yards, 2.8 seconds for 10–19, and 3.1 seconds for 20 or more. EPA per attempt: +0.10 (0–9 yards), +0.39 (10–19), +0.44 (20+); completion rate 72%, 54% and 37%; interception rate 1.6%, 3.2% and 5.0%.

Brown, "One-Trick Pony," *Grantland*, January 25, 2013: in Indianapolis under offensive coordinator Tom Moore the play was called "Dig" ("Levels" to most coaches), with the inside receiver on a square-in or dig and the outside receiver on a five-yard in; Manning ran it "ten times a game in various forms," and 15 or 20 in a big passing game. https://grantland.com/features/how-return-simplicity-peyton-manning-indy-offense-ignited-denver-broncos/

[^heat]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, 2023–2025 regular seasons: 53,346 pass attempts with charted air yards and direction (`pass_location`: left, middle, right), sacks and spikes excluded. The charter's "middle" is roughly the area between the hash marks; it is a judgment call, not a measured coordinate.
